Topic index
How this handbook works

Start here

Read this once before your first lesson. It explains how the stages fit together, how a lesson runs and how students move up.

What this handbook is for

One curriculum, taught the same way in every school, so a student can switch tutors without losing a step.

This handbook covers every topic in NextGen's DJ course across three stages: Warm-Up, Main Room and Headliner. Each topic has a short explanation in plain English, a diagram where a picture helps, the steps to teach it, and what students should be able to do afterwards.

Every topic has a code, such as WU-S02 for Warm-Up skill 2 (beatmatching). Use the codes in your lesson notes so the next tutor knows exactly where a student is.

Talking about the course with families and schools

Describe it as NextGen's three-stage DJ course, with a level-up check and a NextGen certificate at each stage. Don't describe it as accredited, graded or an exam. For students taking GCSE Music, you can say the skills support the DJ performance option in AQA GCSE Music. For other exam boards, check with the school's music department first.

Watch out

This is an internal tutor reference. Please don't share copies with students, families or other organisations.

How we teach

Hands on the decks for most of every lesson, one new idea at a time, and always finish on a win.

  • Play every lesson. Explanation supports playing. It never replaces it.
  • Their music first, then widen it. Start from the tracks a student loves, then bring in new genres once they're hooked.
  • Ears before screens. Waveforms, BPM numbers and sync are tools. Students must learn to hear when something is wrong.
  • One new skill per lesson. Revisit last week's skill before adding another.
  • Move on by skill, not time. Students progress when they pass the level-up check, not after a set number of weeks.

Shape of a 30-minute lesson

TimeWhat happens
0-3 minSet up, headphones on, and a quick ear game (see the Games bank)
3-10 minRevisit last week's skill until it's solid
10-20 minShow the new skill, then a guided try
20-27 minFree play or a challenge that uses the new skill
27-30 minRecap, note progress against the topic code, set something to practise

In paired and group lessons, rotate roles every few minutes: one student mixes, one counts phrases or judges the blend, and one chooses the next track. Everyone keeps listening, and they learn to judge a mix as well as play one.

The three stages

Each stage is named after a slot in a night out. Students start with the Warm-Up, earn the Main Room and finish as the Headliner.

StageFocusLevel-up check
Warm-UpHearing the beat, beatmatching by ear, clean levels and first transitionsA 5-minute mix of three tracks, beatmatched by ear
Main RoomFilters, loops, key, rekordbox prep and reading the roomA 10-12 minute mix across at least two genres
HeadlinerEffects, acapellas, big tempo changes, routines and performingA 15-20 minute set with a planned journey, played to an audience

Every stage is split into Knowledge (what students need to understand), Skills (what they practise on the decks), rekordbox (preparing music), and at Warm-Up, two Genre sessions. Topics marked New are additions that reflect how DJs play in 2026.

Tutor tip

The order within each stage is a sensible default, not a script. Mix Knowledge and Skills topics in the same lesson so students are always playing.

Stage 1 of 3 · 33 topics

The Warm-Up

A complete beginner learns to hear the beat, keep levels clean and mix three tracks together by ear. By the end they can play a short, tidy mix and explain what they're doing.

Level-up check

A 5-minute mix of three tracks of similar tempo, beatmatched by ear, with at least one blend and one cut on the phrase. No bass clashes, no red meters. Then three quick listening questions, such as "Where does the next phrase start?" and "What genre is this?"

Warm-Up

Knowledge

WU-K01

Pulse

The pulse is the steady beat you tap your foot to. Every other DJ skill sits on top of it.

Dance music almost always has four beats in each bar. The first beat of the bar, "the one", is the most important: phrases start on it, drops land on it, and transitions should start on it.

Students don't need to see the beat to feel it. Get them clapping and counting before they touch the decks, then keep coming back to it in every lesson.

What students practise at Warm-Up

  • Clap on every beat in pop, house and hip hop.
  • Clap only on beats 2 and 4 in house (where the clap or snare sits).
  • Clap only on the one in grime, where the drums are less regular.
Game

Find the One. Start a track at a random point. The student counts out loud and claps on the next "one" within four bars. Score a point for each hit.

Teach it
  1. Play a house track and clap on every beat with the student.
  2. Count "1-2-3-4" out loud, stressing the 1.
  3. Switch to clapping only on 2 and 4, then only on the 1.
  4. Repeat with a hip hop track, then a grime track.
Students can
  • Clap in time with the pulse of house, hip hop and pop tracks.
  • Find "the one" within four bars when a track is started at random.
  • Clap on 2 and 4 in a house track.
WU-K02

Beats, bars and phrases

Beats make bars, bars make phrases, and phrases make sections. DJs count in phrases.

A beat is one pulse. A bar is four beats. A phrase is a group of bars, usually 8 or 16 in dance music, often 4 or 8 in hip hop. After each phrase, something changes: a new sound comes in, a drum fill plays, or the track moves into a new section.

Counting phrases is what lets a DJ start the next track at exactly the right moment. If both tracks change at the same time, the mix sounds planned. If they don't, it sounds messy even when the beats are matched.

Tutor tip

Teach students to count bars on their fingers: one finger per bar, so after eight bars their hand is "full" and a change is due.

Teach it
  1. Count beats in a bar together: "1-2-3-4, 2-2-3-4, 3-2-3-4..."
  2. Ask the student to say "change" when they hear something new. Show that it falls after 8 or 16 bars.
  3. Look at the waveform to confirm, but make the ear decide first.
Students can
  • Explain what a beat, a bar and a phrase are.
  • Count bars out loud through a phrase without losing their place.
  • Predict when the next change will come.
WU-K03

Headphones

Headphones let a DJ hear the next track before the crowd does. Learning to use them well is half of beatmatching.

DJ headphones are closed-back, so outside noise is blocked, and most have cups that swivel so the DJ can listen with one ear. The usual technique is one ear on, one ear off: the covered ear hears the next track, the open ear hears the speakers.

Three controls matter. The CUE buttons choose which deck goes to the headphones. The headphone level sets how loud they are. The headphone mix (or cue/master) knob blends between the cued track and what the crowd hears.

Watch out

Set the headphone level before pressing play, and keep it moderate. Students often turn headphones up to hear over the speakers, and that's when ears get damaged. Turn the room speakers down instead.

Teach it
  1. Show how to wear them with one ear on and one ear off, and how to swap sides.
  2. Press CUE on the deck that isn't playing and show that only the student hears it.
  3. Turn the headphone mix fully to cue, then fully to master, then to the middle.
  4. Set a safe headphone level together and explain why.
Students can
  • Choose which deck they hear in their headphones.
  • Use one-ear monitoring comfortably.
  • Set a safe headphone volume without being told.
WU-K04

Harmonic mixing: first steps

Every melodic track is written in a key. Two tracks in keys that clash will sound wrong together, even if the beats are perfect.

A key is the family of notes a track's melody, chords and bassline are built from. When two tracks share most of their notes, they blend smoothly. When they don't, the mix sounds sour.

rekordbox works out the key of each track when it analyses it. Most DJs use the Camelot system, which gives each key a number from 1 to 12 and a letter: A for minor keys, B for major. Neighbouring numbers sound good together.

The simple rule for Warm-Up

Stay on the same number, move one number up or down, or swap between A and B on the same number. That covers most good-sounding mixes.

Tutor tip

Don't let key rules slow down beginners. At Warm-Up, play two clashing tracks and two matching ones so students hear the difference, then move on. It becomes a proper skill at Main Room (MR-K15).

Teach it
  1. Play two tracks with clashing keys over each other. Ask how it sounds.
  2. Play two tracks with matching keys. Ask again.
  3. Show where rekordbox displays the key and how the Camelot number works.
Students can
  • Hear when two melodic tracks clash.
  • Find a track's key in rekordbox.
  • Pick a matching track using the same or neighbouring Camelot number.
WU-K05

The cue button

The cue button marks where a track will start and lets you jump back there instantly. It's how every transition begins.

On most decks and controllers, the CUE button does three things, depending on what the deck is doing:

  • Paused: pressing CUE saves the current position as the cue point.
  • Playing: pressing CUE jumps back to the cue point and stops.
  • At the cue point: holding CUE plays the track for as long as it's held. Letting go jumps back to the cue point.

That last behaviour is how DJs "stutter" the start of a track in time with the music, then press PLAY to let it run.

Cueing up a track

  1. Load the track and find the first beat by turning the jog wheel.
  2. With the deck paused, press CUE to save that point.
  3. Hold CUE to check it starts on the beat. Let go to jump back.
  4. When the moment comes, press PLAY on the beat.
Watch out

Don't confuse the deck CUE button with the headphone CUE button on the mixer. One sets a starting point, the other chooses what's in your headphones.

Teach it
  1. Show the three behaviours one at a time.
  2. Have the student set a cue on the first kick of a track.
  3. Practise starting the track on the one while another track plays.
Students can
  • Set a cue point on the first beat.
  • Return to it instantly.
  • Start the track exactly on the one.
WU-K06

Sections of a track

Club tracks are built from sections that each last a set number of bars. Knowing them tells you when to mix in and out.

Most dance tracks follow a familiar pattern. The intro is stripped back so DJs can mix into it. A build-up adds tension. The drop (or chorus) is the high point. A breakdown removes the drums for a moment of calm. Then a second build and drop, and finally an outro for mixing out.

Songs with vocals often use verse, pre-chorus, chorus instead. The idea is the same: sections change on the phrase.

In the lesson

In lessons we use La Danza as the class example. Play it and have students call out each section as it arrives, then check against the waveform.

Teach it
  1. Play a whole track and have the student name each section as it arrives.
  2. Count the bars in each section together.
  3. Point out where the intro and outro give space to mix.
Students can
  • Name the main sections of a club track and a song.
  • Recognise a build-up, drop and breakdown by ear.
  • Say how many bars a section lasts.
WU-K07

Components of electronic music

Every dance track is built from the same few ingredients. Hearing them separately makes EQ and mixing make sense.

Kick drumThe low thud you feel in your chest. Every beat in house, looser in hip hop and grime.
Snare or clapA short, sharp crack, usually on beats 2 and 4.
Hi-hatA tight "tss" closed, a longer sizzle open. Keeps time moving between the beats.
BasslineThe low notes that carry the groove, locked to the kick.
MelodyThe tune you remember: synths, keys, guitars.
VocalsAnything sung, rapped or spoken: verses, choruses, hooks.

Three beats to know

Game

Name That Part. Play eight bars. The student points at the kick, then the clap, then the hats, by tapping along to each one in turn.

Teach it
  1. Play a house loop and tap along to just the kick, then just the clap, then just the hats.
  2. Compare the house pattern with a hip hop and a grime pattern.
  3. Use the EQ to remove the low end and ask what disappeared.
Students can
  • Pick out the kick, snare or clap, hats, bass, melody and vocals by ear.
  • Describe the basic house drum pattern.
  • Hear the difference between house, hip hop and grime rhythms.
WU-K08

Setting up and signal flow

Sound travels in one direction: from where the music is stored, through the player and mixer, out to the speakers. When something goes wrong, follow that path.

Powering up and down

Speakers are the last thing on and the first thing off. That avoids a loud pop that can damage them.

  1. Faders and master level all the way down. Gains at the middle (12 o'clock).
  2. Plug in the controller and laptop. Open rekordbox.
  3. Turn the controller on, then the speakers last.
  4. To finish: faders down, speakers off first, then the controller.

Cables you'll meet

  • USB: connects a controller to the laptop, or a USB stick to a player.
  • RCA (red and white): carries left and right audio from a controller to speakers. Red goes in the right-hand socket.
  • XLR and jack: used by club mixers and powered speakers.
  • Power: check the right voltage and never trail cables where people walk.
Teach it
  1. Trace the signal path on your setup, pointing at each stage.
  2. Have the student power up in the right order.
  3. Unplug one cable and ask them to find the fault.
Students can
  • Name the four stages of signal flow.
  • Power the setup up and down safely.
  • Find a simple fault by following the signal path.
WU-K09

Equipment functions

Every controller has the same core controls, just arranged differently. Learn what each does, and any setup becomes familiar.

ControlWhat it does
Jog wheelNudges a track faster or slower to line it up. Touching the top scratches.
Tempo sliderChanges the track's speed as a percentage of its original BPM
Play/pauseStarts and stops the track
CueSets and returns to the cue point (see WU-K05)
Performance padsHot cues, loops and samples
Browse and loadScrolls through music and loads a track onto a deck
Trim (gain)Sets how loud the track comes into the mixer
EQ: high, mid, lowTurns frequency bands up or down
Filter (colour FX)Sweeps away lows or highs
Headphone cueSends that channel to the headphones
Channel faderControls how much of that channel goes to the master
CrossfaderBlends between the left and right decks

Also find master level (overall volume to the speakers), headphone level, headphone mix, and master tempo or key lock, which keeps a track's pitch the same when you change its speed.

Teach it
  1. Go round the controller with the numbered table, one area at a time.
  2. Ask the student to find each control without looking at the table.
  3. Explain master tempo by changing the tempo with it on and off.
Students can
  • Name and use every control on the diagram.
  • Explain the difference between trim, channel fader and master level.
WU-K10

EQ

EQ splits a track into low, mid and high frequencies so you can make room for the next track. Its most important job is stopping two basslines clashing.

Each channel has three EQ knobs. At 12 o'clock they're neutral. Turn left to cut, right to boost. Cutting is far more useful than boosting.

The bass swap

Two basslines or kick drums playing at once turn muddy and boom through the speakers. So during a blend, only one track should have its low EQ up at any moment. The classic move is to swap them on a phrase: the incoming track's lows come up exactly as the outgoing track's lows go down.

Tutor tip

Teach "EQ to cut, not to boost". If a student wants more bass, the answer is usually less bass in the other track.

Teach it
  1. Sweep each EQ band on one track so the student hears what it controls.
  2. Blend two tracks with both lows up and listen to the mud.
  3. Practise a bass swap on a phrase change.
Students can
  • Explain what the low, mid and high EQ control.
  • Keep only one bassline playing at a time during a blend.
  • Make a clean bass swap on the phrase.
WU-K11

Genres at Warm-Up

Genres tell you a track's speed, its rhythm and how to mix it. Warm-Up starts with the four most students already know.

GenreTypical BPMWhere and whenMixing it
Pop and commercial90-130Everywhere, all erasShort intros: use the outro or a clean cut
House120-128Chicago, 1980sLong beat intros: perfect for first blends
Hip hop and rap85-100New York, 1970sShort and vocal-led: quick blends and cuts
Grime138-142East London, early 2000sHard cuts on the phrase, built for MCs
Afrobeats95-115Nigeria and Ghana, 2000s onBlend over percussion, avoid vocals clashing

Pop and commercial music isn't one style. It's whatever's in the charts, so it borrows from every genre. Its tracks are short, with verses and choruses rather than long DJ intros.

Tutor tip

Students can play any genre at any stage. This table is about when we teach each genre's history and mixing quirks.

WU-K12

House

House is the foundation of club music: a steady kick on every beat, made for dancing all night.

Tempo
120-128 BPM
Born
Chicago, early 1980s
Rhythm
Four to the floor
Sound
Soulful, repetitive, uplifting
Grew out of
DiscoSoul and gospelSynth-pop and electro
House
Led to
Acid houseDeep houseUK garageTech houseAfro house

Brief history

House grew out of disco in Chicago. After the 1979 backlash killed disco on the radio, Chicago's Black and gay club scene kept dancing to it. At a club called the Warehouse, resident DJ Frankie Knuckles mixed disco, soul and electronic records into long, unbroken sets, re-editing tracks and adding drum machine beats. Record shops started labelling that sound "Warehouse music", soon shortened to "house".

Local producers began making their own tracks on cheap drum machines such as the Roland TR-808 and TR-909. Jesse Saunders' "On and On" (1984) is often called the first house record. Ron Hardy at the Music Box played a rawer, wilder version, and in 1987 Phuture's "Acid Tracks" used the squelching Roland TB-303 to invent acid house.

By 1988 house had crossed to the UK, where acid house fuelled the rave scene and the "Second Summer of Love". Today it splits into many styles, including deep house, tech house, Afro house and garage-influenced house, and it's back in the charts.

What to listen for

  • A four-to-the-floor kick at 120-128 BPM that never lets up.
  • Claps or snares on 2 and 4, with open hi-hats on the offbeat.
  • Soulful or gospel-style vocals, piano chords and short repeating loops.
  • Long intros and outros built for DJs to mix over.
  • A positive, uplifting mood, often in major keys.

Artists who shaped it

FKFrankie Knuckles"The Godfather of House", resident at the Warehouse
RHRon HardyMusic Box DJ known for raw, high-energy edits
MJMarshall JeffersonMade "Move Your Body", the house anthem
LHLarry Heard (Mr. Fingers)Created deep house with "Can You Feel It"
PPhutureDiscovered the acid sound of the TB-303
MAMasters at WorkLouie Vega and Kenny Dope, who shaped New York house

Key artists now

FAFred again..Emotional, vocal-sampling house that fills arenas
PGPeggy GouKorean-born DJ with chart-topping house hits
HDHoney DijonChicago-born DJ keeping the original sound alive
DDisclosureUK duo who brought house back to the charts in the 2010s
Tunes that shaped it
  • Frankie Knuckles & Jamie PrincipleYour Love (1987)
  • Mr. FingersCan You Feel It (1986)
  • Marshall JeffersonMove Your Body (1986)
  • Robin SShow Me Love (1993)
  • Daft PunkOne More Time (2000)
  • Fred again..Delilah (pull me out of this) (2022)
  • Peggy Gou(It Goes Like) Nanana (2023)
Students can
  • Recognise house by its four-to-the-floor beat.
  • Tell the story of where house came from in two or three sentences.
  • Name two pioneers and two current house artists.
  • Mix two house tracks with a long blend.
WU-K13

Hip hop and rap

Hip hop began with a DJ. Its first records were built from looped drum breaks, and the DJ was the star before the MC.

Tempo
85-100 BPM
Born
The Bronx, New York, 1973
Rhythm
Swung "boom bap", snare on 2 and 4
Sound
Vocal-led, sampled, punchy
Grew out of
Funk and soul breaksJamaican sound systemsDisco
Hip hop
Led to
Boom bapGangsta rapTrapUK rapDrill

Brief history

In August 1973, DJ Kool Herc, who had grown up around Jamaica's sound system culture, threw a party in the Bronx. He noticed dancers went wild for the short instrumental "breaks" in funk records, so he used two copies of the same record to repeat the break again and again. Grandmaster Flash refined the technique, Grand Wizzard Theodore is credited with discovering the scratch, and MCs began rapping over the beats. Afrika Bambaataa's Zulu Nation used the parties to steer young people away from gangs.

Hip hop grew from four elements: DJing, MCing, breakdancing and graffiti. Run-DMC took it mainstream in the 1980s. The 1990s "golden era" brought sampling and lyricism on both coasts, from Nas and the Notorious B.I.G. in New York to Dr. Dre and Snoop Dogg in Los Angeles. Since the 2010s, trap production and streaming have made hip hop the world's most listened-to genre.

UK rap has its own sound and stars. Dave won the Mercury Prize in 2019 and Little Simz in 2022.

What to listen for

  • Rapped vocals telling stories over a beat.
  • Beats built from samples of funk, soul and jazz records.
  • Boom bap drums: a swung kick and a hard snare on 2 and 4.
  • Modern tracks borrow trap's 808 bass and rolling hi-hats.
  • Scratches and DJ cuts on classic tracks.

Artists who shaped it

KHDJ Kool HercLooped the breaks and started it all
GFGrandmaster FlashPerfected cutting between records
ABAfrika BambaataaZulu Nation and the electro hit "Planet Rock"
RRun-DMCTook hip hop into the mainstream
DDDr. DreDefined the West Coast sound as a producer
JDJ DillaLoose, off-grid drums that changed beat-making

Key artists now

KLKendrick LamarPulitzer Prize-winning US rapper
DDaveMercury Prize-winning South London rapper
LSLittle SimzMercury Prize-winning North London rapper
CCCentral CeeUK rapper with global streaming hits
Tunes that shaped it
  • The Sugarhill GangRapper's Delight (1979)
  • Grandmaster Flash & the Furious FiveThe Message (1982)
  • Run-DMCWalk This Way (1986)
  • NasN.Y. State of Mind (1994)
  • The Notorious B.I.G.Juicy (1994)
  • Kendrick LamarHUMBLE. (2017)
  • Dave ft. FredoFunky Friday (2018)
Students can
  • Explain how DJs created hip hop.
  • Recognise a boom bap beat.
  • Name a hip hop pioneer, a UK artist and a US artist.
WU-K14

Grime

Grime is London's own sound: fast, raw and built around MCs, born on pirate radio in the early 2000s.

Tempo
Around 140 BPM
Born
East London, early 2000s
Rhythm
Sparse, broken, syncopated
Sound
Dark synths, heavy bass, MCs
Grew out of
UK garageJungleDancehallHip hop
Grime
Led to
UK drillUK rapAfroswing

Brief history

Grime came out of UK garage when a younger generation of MCs in Bow and the surrounding East London estates wanted something harder. Wiley, Dizzee Rascal and crews such as Roll Deep made instrumentals at about 140 BPM on basic software such as FruityLoops, and played them on pirate radio stations like Rinse FM, at raves and in recorded MC clashes. Dizzee Rascal's album Boy in da Corner won the Mercury Prize in 2003.

A second wave in the mid-2010s, led by Skepta, Stormzy and JME, took grime to the top of the charts. Skepta's Konnichiwa won the Mercury Prize in 2016, and in 2019 Stormzy headlined Glastonbury. UK drill later grew from the same scene.

What to listen for

  • A tempo of about 140 BPM, with lots of space in the beat.
  • Sparse, broken drums rather than a steady kick.
  • Cold, square-wave synths and heavy basslines.
  • Fast MCs, usually in 8- and 16-bar verses.
  • Built for pirate radio, clashes and reloads.

The grime DJ

Grime DJs work with MCs. They cut tracks in hard on the phrase, and when a tune goes off they reload it (also called a rewind or wheel-up): spin it back and start it again. Short mixes and quick changes keep the energy high.

Artists who shaped it

WWiley"The Godfather of Grime" and his "eskibeat" sound
DRDizzee RascalFirst grime album to win the Mercury Prize
RDRoll DeepThe crew that launched Wiley, Skepta and more
KKanoEarly teen star who became one of its best lyricists
LBLethal B"Pow!", the anthem that got banned from clubs
DDD Double EOne of the most copied MC styles

Key artists now

SSkeptaLed the second wave, Mercury Prize winner
SStormzyGlastonbury headliner and chart-topping album artist
JJMEBoy Better Know co-founder and independent pioneer
NNovelistLewisham MC and producer keeping it raw
Tunes that shaped it
  • WileyEskimo (2002)
  • Dizzee RascalI Luv U (2003)
  • WileyWot Do U Call It? (2004)
  • Lethal BPow! (Forward) (2004)
  • SkeptaShutdown (2015)
  • StormzyShut Up (2015)
Students can
  • Recognise grime by its tempo and sparse beats.
  • Explain where grime came from and name two pioneers.
  • Describe what a reload is.
WU-K15

Afrobeats

New

Afrobeats is the sound of modern Nigeria and Ghana: bouncing percussion and melodic vocals, and one of the biggest genres in UK schools.

Tempo
95-115 BPM
Born
Lagos and Accra, 2000s
Rhythm
Syncopated, rolling percussion
Sound
Melodic vocals, warm grooves
Grew out of
HighlifeFela Kuti's AfrobeatHip hop and R&BDancehall
Afrobeats
Led to
AfroswingAltéAfrobeats-amapiano crossovers

Brief history

Afrobeats mixes West African highlife and percussion with hip hop, R&B and dancehall. Don't confuse it with Afrobeat (no "s"), the 1970s style of horns, funk and politics created in Lagos by Fela Kuti.

In the 2000s, Nigerian pop stars such as 2Face Idibia and D'banj built a new sound that spread across Africa and the diaspora. UK DJs, including DJ Abrantee, helped popularise the name "Afrobeats" around 2011, and D'banj's "Oliver Twist" reached the UK top 10. Then Wizkid featured on Drake's "One Dance" (2016), and the sound went global. Burna Boy won a Grammy in 2021, and Rema's "Calm Down" became one of the most streamed songs in the world.

In the UK it shaped Afroswing, a mix of Afrobeats and UK rap from artists such as J Hus and NSG.

What to listen for

  • Mid-tempo grooves around 95-115 BPM.
  • Syncopated kicks that skip across the bar, with constant shakers.
  • Sung, melodic vocals in English, Pidgin, Yoruba, Twi and more.
  • A relaxed, danceable feel rather than big drops.
  • Short intros, often starting straight on the vocal.

Artists who shaped it

FKFela KutiCreated Afrobeat, the music it grew from
2I2Face Idibia"African Queen", an early pan-African hit
DD'banj"Oliver Twist", an early UK chart breakthrough
PP-SquareTwin brothers who made Afropop huge across Africa
WWizkidTook the sound global with "One Dance"
ADJ AbranteeUK DJ who helped popularise the name

Key artists now

BBBurna BoyGrammy winner and stadium headliner
TTemsGrammy-winning singer and songwriter
RRema"Calm Down", one of the world's biggest songs
AAsakeBlends Afrobeats with amapiano and Yoruba chants
Tunes that shaped it
  • Fela KutiWater No Get Enemy (1975)
  • 2Face IdibiaAfrican Queen (2004)
  • D'banjOliver Twist (2011)
  • WizkidOjuelegba (2014)
  • Drake ft. Wizkid & KylaOne Dance (2016)
  • Wizkid ft. TemsEssence (2020)
  • Rema & Selena GomezCalm Down (2022)
Tutor tip

Afrobeats tracks often start with vocals and have short intros. Mix on percussion-only sections and avoid laying two vocals on top of each other.

Students can
  • Tell Afrobeats from Afrobeat.
  • Name two artists who took Afrobeats global.
  • Mix two Afrobeats tracks without clashing vocals.
WU-K16

Where to transition

Start the next track at the beginning of a phrase, and finish the old one before its next big moment. That one rule fixes most beginner mixes.

  • Good: at the end of a drop or chorus, so the energy has been released.
  • Good: in the outro, so the crowd has heard the whole track.
  • Good: at the start of any phrase, so the two tracks change together.
  • Avoid: halfway through a section, especially a chorus.
  • Avoid: during a build-up. The crowd is waiting for a drop, and a new track confuses that.
  • Avoid: changing tracks too quickly. Let the crowd hear a track properly.
Game

Phrase Spotter. Play a track. The student calls "change" just before each new phrase. Count the hits out of ten.

Students can
  • Choose a sensible point to start the next track.
  • Explain why mixing during a build-up feels wrong.
WU-K17

Improvisation

Improvising means deciding what to play next while you're playing. Most DJs prepare some of a set and improvise the rest.

The most common improvisation is track selection. Instead of planning every track, the DJ listens to how the last one went down and chooses the next to suit. That lets the set respond to the room.

Preparation has its place too: a planned run of tracks can be rehearsed until the transitions are perfect. A good set uses both.

Preparation gives youImprovisation gives you
Tight, rehearsed transitionsA set that responds to the crowd
Confidence under pressureSurprise and personality
Tricky mixes that need practiceFreedom to change direction
Tutor tip

Give beginners a short pool of six tracks that all mix together. They choose the order live, so improvisation feels safe.

Students can
  • Explain the difference between preparing and improvising.
  • Choose the next track live from a small pool.
WU-K18

Structuring a mix

A mix is a journey, and energy is what moves it. Every track has an energy level, and the order you play them in shapes how the set feels.

A mix is a run of tracks blended into one continuous piece. Energy is how much lift a track gives the listener: tempo, how full the sound is, the drums, the mood. It depends on what came before, too: a mid-energy track feels huge after a quiet one.

At Warm-Up, students rate each track from 1 (chilled) to 5 (peak), then plan an order that rises and falls on purpose.

Game

Energy Line-Up. Give the student five tracks. They rank them 1 to 5 for energy, then justify one choice out loud.

Students can
  • Say which of two tracks has more energy, and why.
  • Rate tracks 1 to 5 and plan a three-track mix that builds.
WU-K19

Finding music and curation

A DJ is only as good as their music. Curation means finding tracks you love, and knowing why they belong together.

Every track is a lead to more music. From one track you know its artist, its label, its genre and its remixers. Each opens up more: the artist's other releases, the label's catalogue, charts in that genre, and mixes by DJs who play it.

Where to look

  • DJ stores and charts: Beatport, Bandcamp, Traxsource and Juno Download sort music by genre and publish charts.
  • Mixes and radio: BBC Radio 1 specialist shows, SoundCloud and Mixcloud. Use the tracklist or a recognition app to identify songs.
  • Labels and artists: follow them on streaming platforms and social media for new releases.

Quality matters

Big speakers make bad files sound terrible. Use WAV, AIFF, FLAC or 320kbps MP3. Avoid anything below 192kbps, and never use files ripped from YouTube or other video sites.

Watch out

In school, check lyrics and use clean versions. A track that's fine at home might not be fine in an assembly.

Students can
  • Find new music starting from one track they like.
  • Explain why file quality matters.
  • Name two legal places to buy or stream music for DJing.
WU-K20

Online stores and rekordbox

Students need a legal, reliable way to get music into rekordbox. This lesson goes from buying a track to having it ready on a deck.

Buying and importing

  1. Buy the track from a DJ store and download the highest quality file offered.
  2. Save it in one music folder, not scattered across Downloads.
  3. In rekordbox, import the file or folder, or drag it into the collection.
  4. Wait for rekordbox to analyse it. That finds the BPM, key and beat grid.
  5. Add it to a playlist so it's easy to find in a lesson.

Streaming services

rekordbox can also stream tracks directly from services such as Beatport, Beatsource, SoundCloud and TIDAL with the right subscription. Streaming needs a reliable internet connection, and the DJ doesn't own the music. We cover the pros and cons at Headliner (HL-R01).

Tutor tip

Agree with families what students can buy, and point them to the office for current recommendations. Never share your own purchased music with students.

Teach it
  1. Walk through buying, downloading and importing one track.
  2. Show where rekordbox stores the analysed BPM and key.
  3. Make a playlist for the student's next lesson.
Students can
  • Import a track and confirm it's been analysed.
  • Explain the difference between owning and streaming music.
Warm-Up

Skills

WU-S01

Intro types

Not every track starts with a beat. Spotting the type of intro tells you how to mix the track in.

IntroWhat it sounds likeHow to mix it
Beat introDrums from the first bar, often for 8 to 32 barsThe easiest. Cue the first beat and beatmatch as normal.
Beatless or FX introPads, noise or effects with no drumsHard to beatmatch. Cue where the beat starts, or line up any rhythmic sound.
Acapella introJust a voiceLine up the vocal with the other track's beat, or cue the track after the vocal.
Students can
  • Recognise each intro type.
  • Choose a sensible cue point for each.
WU-S02

Beatmatching

Beatmatching makes two tracks play at the same speed with their beats lined up, so they sound like one. It's the core skill of DJing.

Two things have to be right. The tempo must match, or the beats drift apart. And the beats must be lined up, or they clatter even at the same tempo. At Warm-Up, students can read the BPM numbers to set the tempo, but the lining up must be done by ear.

The Warm-Up beatmatching routine

  1. Play track A. Load track B and set its tempo to match A's BPM.
  2. Cue B on its first beat.
  3. Count A's bars in your head and press PLAY on B on the one at the start of a phrase.
  4. Listen in the headphones. Is B ahead (rushing) or behind (dragging)?
  5. Nudge B's jog wheel by its outer edge: spin forward if behind, slow it if ahead.
  6. When the kicks sound like one kick, bring B in.
Tutor tip

If the beats keep drifting after you've lined them up, the tempo is wrong. The jog wheel only nudges. The tempo slider fixes drift.

Game

Drift Detective. You nudge one deck out of line. The student says "ahead" or "behind", then fixes it.

Teach it
  1. Use two copies of the same track first, so only alignment matters.
  2. Then two different house tracks with the same BPM.
  3. Cover the waveforms for the last few tries.
Students can
  • Start a track on the one, at the start of a phrase.
  • Hear whether a track is ahead or behind.
  • Line up two tracks by ear and keep them together for a phrase.
WU-S03

Cue points

A good cue point is exactly on the first beat you want to hear. If it's a fraction early or late, every mix starts badly.

Zoom in on the waveform and set the cue on the front edge of the first kick, not the middle of it. Then check by ear: hold CUE and listen for a clean, instant thud.

Pick the cue point for the job:

  • First beat of the intro: for a long blend.
  • First beat of the drop: for a cut straight into the big moment.
  • After an acapella or FX intro: when the start has no beat to match.
Students can
  • Set a cue exactly on the first beat.
  • Choose a cue point that suits the transition they're planning.
WU-S04

Transitions

A transition is how you get from one track to the next. Warm-Up teaches the two families: cuts and blends.

Cuts

A straight cut switches from the old track to the new one instantly, on the first beat of a phrase. It's quick, punchy and common in hip hop and grime.

A beat cut teases the new track first: flick the crossfader or fader in on single beats, then cut fully across on the phrase. It builds excitement for the next tune.

Blends

A blend plays both tracks together for a while. Warm-Up students learn blends over one, two and four phrases.

Tutor tip

Ask students to say the plan before they start: "I'll bring it in over one phrase and swap the bass at bar 9." Planning out loud fixes most timing mistakes.

Teach it
  1. Start with straight cuts on the phrase until timing is reliable.
  2. Add the beat cut for fun.
  3. Move to one-phrase blends with a bass swap, then two and four.
Students can
  • Make a straight cut and a beat cut on the phrase.
  • Make one-, two- and four-phrase blends with a clean bass swap.
WU-S05

Baby scratch

The baby scratch is the first scratch everyone learns: push the record forward and pull it back, in time, with the fader open.

Use the hand on the jog wheel only. Rest your fingers lightly on the top of the wheel at about 9 o'clock with the wrist raised, and move it forward and back over the start of a sound. Every scratch in this handbook builds on this movement.

Setting up to scratch

  • Use a long sound, such as a held vocal "ahhh" or a horn note.
  • Set a cue point at the very start of the sound.
  • Set the crossfader curve to sharp (see MR-K05).
  • Play a simple hip hop beat at about 90 BPM on the other deck.
Teach it
  1. Push forward on beat 1 and pull back on beat 2, then speed up to two per beat.
  2. Keep strokes the same length so the sound is consistent.
Students can
  • Perform a steady baby scratch in time with a beat.
WU-S06

Drop cut

A drop cut plays a sound at normal speed, then cuts it off with the fader before you pull it back, so the crowd only hears the sound going forward.

Release the jog wheel so the sample plays, open the fader for one beat, then close it. Bring the sample back to the start while the fader is closed, ready for the next drop.

Teach it
  1. Find the start of the sample with the fader closed.
  2. Open the fader and release the wheel on the beat.
  3. Close the fader on the next beat, then pull back silently.
Students can
  • Drop a sample in time, cutting it cleanly each time.
WU-S07

Forward cut

The forward cut is a baby scratch with the backward stroke silenced. You only hear the push.

Push the sound forward with the fader open, close the fader, then pull back. It gives a sharper, cleaner sound than a baby scratch and is the building block for faster cutting scratches later.

Students can
  • Perform forward cuts on every beat, then on every half beat.
WU-S08

Drop scratch

A drop scratch lets the sound play forward, then catches it and pulls it back so you hear both directions.

The fader stays open. Release the wheel to play the sample, catch it, and pull it back to the start in rhythm. It sits between a drop cut and a baby scratch, and works well over slower hip hop beats.

Students can
  • Perform drop scratches in time with a beat.
WU-S09

Beat juggling: jog wheel loop

Beat juggling remixes a beat live by switching between two copies of the same track. The jog wheel loop is the first and simplest juggle.

Load the same track on both decks. Play a four-beat section on one deck. While it plays, spin the other deck back to the start of the same section, then cut across with the crossfader exactly as the first deck finishes. Repeat, switching sides each time, and the section loops for as long as you can keep up.

  1. Load the same track on both decks and cue both at the same bar.
  2. Play deck A for four beats with the crossfader on A.
  3. Cut to deck B on the next beat and let it play.
  4. While B plays, spin A back to the start of the section.
  5. Cut back to A after four beats. Keep switching.
Tutor tip

Start with an eight-beat section and shorten it as the student gets quicker. This is exactly what Grandmaster Flash was doing in the 1970s, which makes a good story for the lesson.

Students can
  • Loop a four-beat section for at least four repeats in time.
Warm-Up

rekordbox

WU-R01

Getting around rekordbox

rekordbox is where DJs prepare and play their music. Students need to find their way around it before anything else.

  • Decks and waveforms: show each track, where it's playing and what's coming next.
  • Track info: title, artist, BPM and key for each loaded track.
  • Tree view (left): the collection, playlists and connected devices.
  • Browser (middle): the tracks in whatever is selected in the tree view.
Tutor tip

rekordbox's layout changes between versions and modes. Always teach on the version the student will use at home.

Students can
  • Find a track, load it to a deck and read its BPM and key.
WU-R02

Music management

A tidy library means finding the right track in seconds. A messy one means panic in the middle of a set.

  • Playlists hold tracks for a purpose: a genre, a set, a lesson.
  • Folders hold playlists, so the tree view stays short.
  • File names should be clear: Artist - Title (Remix).
  1. Click the + next to Playlists to create one, and name it clearly.
  2. Drag tracks in from the collection.
  3. Right-click Playlists to create a folder, and drag playlists into it.
Students can
  • Create playlists and folders and keep them organised.
  • Name files clearly and consistently.
Warm-Up

Genre sessions

WU-G01

Mixing hip hop

Hip hop tracks are short, vocal-heavy and full of character. Mix them quickly, cleanly and with a bit of attitude.

  • Keep blends short. Long blends make two sets of vocals clash. Blend for four or eight bars at most.
  • Cut on the phrase. Hip hop phrases are often four or eight bars. Cut on the one at the end of a verse or hook.
  • Use the intro or hook. Drop the new track in on its hook for an instant reaction.
  • Mind the tempo. Hip hop sits around 85-100 BPM. Bigger jumps sound unnatural.
  • Add flair. A baby scratch or quick beat cut on the way in suits the genre.
Game

Hook Swap. Play six hip hop tracks. The student must bring each one in on its hook, cutting on the phrase, without a vocal clash.

Students can
  • Mix hip hop tracks with short blends and clean cuts.
  • Bring a track in on its hook.
WU-G02

Mixing grime

Grime is mixed fast and hard. The crowd and the MCs want energy, not long blends.

  • Hard cuts on the phrase. Grime phrases are usually 8 or 16 bars.
  • Count in 16s. MCs often spit 16-bar verses, so the DJ changes tracks between them.
  • Reload the big tunes. When a track goes off, stop it with a quick backspin or by pulling the record, and start it again.
  • Keep it moving. Play one or two minutes of each track at most.
Watch out

Check lyrics carefully. Many grime tracks have explicit versions. Use clean versions in school.

Students can
  • Cut grime tracks cleanly on the phrase.
  • Perform a reload at a sensible moment.
Stage 2 of 3 · 37 topics

The Main Room

Students who can already mix learn to shape a set: setting the tempo by ear, using filters and loops, choosing tracks in compatible keys, preparing music properly and reacting to the crowd.

Level-up check

A 10-12 minute mix of four or five tracks across at least two genres, with tempo set by ear. It must include at least one filter or loop transition and one key choice the student can explain, with levels steady throughout. Then the student talks you through their set plan in under a minute.

Main Room

Knowledge

MR-K01

Pulse: going deeper

At Main Room, students stop just following the beat and start predicting it: where a phrase starts, where a section changes, where the offbeat sits.

Main Room adds more genres with different feels, so the pulse exercises widen too.

Genre groupStudents clap on
House, tech house, techno, discoA beat you name, such as bar 2, beat 3. The first beat of every phrase. The first beat of each new section. The offbeat ("and") between kicks.
Hip hop, grime, trap, R&BThe pulse, and the first beat of each bar, even when the kick isn't on it
Tutor tip

Clapping the offbeat is harder than it sounds. Count "1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and" and clap on every "and". It's the same place the open hi-hat sits in house.

Game

Call the Beat. You shout a bar and beat, such as "bar 3, beat 2". The student claps exactly there while the track plays.

Students can
  • Clap on a named beat within four bars.
  • Clap on the first beat of each phrase and each new section.
  • Clap on the offbeat in house and techno.
MR-K02

Phrase change signals

Producers signal that a phrase is ending, so listeners feel the change coming. DJs who hear these signals never get lost.

Small signals mark the end of a phrase. Bigger ones mark the end of a section. Listen for:

  • Drum fills: a few extra snare or tom hits in the last bar.
  • Dropped beats: the kick cuts out for a beat or a bar.
  • Risers and sweeps: a rising noise or whoosh that builds tension.
  • Crash cymbals: a crash on the first beat of a new phrase.
  • Vocal pickups: a word or phrase leading into the next section.
  • Snare rolls: snare hits getting faster before a drop.

In tracks without vocals or melody, it can help to label contrasting sections A, B and C rather than verse and chorus.

Game

Signal Spotter. Play a track. The student names the signal they hear at each phrase change: fill, riser, dropped beat or crash.

Students can
  • Name at least three phrase signals and hear them in a track.
  • Tell a phrase ending from a section ending.
MR-K03

Components of electronic music: the full kit

Main Room students learn the rest of the drum kit and the instruments producers use to build tracks.

TomsPitched drums (high, mid, low), often used for fills.
Crash cymbalA big splash that marks the start of a phrase or section.
Ride cymbalA lighter, ringing cymbal played on every beat to drive a track forward.
ShakerA rolling rhythm that fills the gaps between the beats.
CowbellA hollow, high "tonk" common in house, disco and Latin music.
Drum machinePlays programmed drum patterns. The TR-808 and TR-909 are the famous ones.
SamplerRecords or loads sounds and plays them back, chopped and rearranged.
SynthesiserCreates sounds electronically, with controls to shape pitch, tone and movement.
Students can
  • Identify toms, crash, ride, shaker and cowbell by ear.
  • Explain what a drum machine, sampler and synthesiser do.
MR-K04

Signal flow inside the mixer

Each mixer channel processes the sound in a fixed order. Knowing that order explains why trim comes before EQ, and why the cue still works with the fader down.

  • Input selector: chooses the source. Line is for media players, phono is for turntables (the record's signal needs boosting and correcting), and USB or digital is for computers.
  • Trim: sets the level coming into the channel.
  • EQ: shapes the frequencies.
  • Channel meter: shows the level after trim and EQ.
  • Channel fader and crossfader: decide how much reaches the master.
  • Outputs: master out to the main speakers, booth out to the DJ's monitor speakers, rec out to a recorder.
Watch out

Plugging a turntable into a line input sounds thin and quiet. Plugging a media player into a phono input sounds horribly loud and distorted. Check the input selector first when something sounds wrong.

Students can
  • Put the stages of a mixer channel in order.
  • Explain the difference between line and phono inputs, and master and booth outputs.
MR-K05

Equipment functions: going deeper

Main Room students use more of the controller: the crossfader properly, the loop controls and quantise.

Crossfader

The crossfader blends the decks assigned to its left and right sides. In the middle, both play. Its curve sets how quickly the sound changes as it moves. A smooth curve is for blending. A sharp curve opens a deck fully after only a tiny movement, which is what scratch DJs need.

Loop controls

  • Loop in: sets where a loop starts.
  • Loop out: sets where it ends, and the track starts repeating.
  • Reloop or exit: leaves the loop, or jumps back into it.
  • Auto beat loop: loops a set number of beats instantly, such as 4 or 8.

Quantise

Snaps cue points, hot cues and loops to the nearest beat (see MR-K14).

Tutor tip

Ask students to explain sync and then not use it for this stage. Sync is useful, but a Main Room DJ should be able to match tempos by ear first.

Students can
  • Change the crossfader curve and explain when to use each setting.
  • Set a manual loop and an auto beat loop.
MR-K06

Levels and gain staging

Every part of the setup can only handle so much signal. Too much and it distorts. Setting levels properly keeps the music loud, clean and even from track to track.

Three controls affect volume, in this order:

  1. Trim: the level coming in. Set this first.
  2. Channel fader: how much of that channel goes to the master.
  3. Master level: the overall volume to the speakers.

Setting a track's level

  1. Look at the waveform. A thin waveform means a quieter track.
  2. Play the loudest part (the widest part of the waveform).
  3. Set trim so the meter sits around the last green light, flickering into amber.
  4. Compare with the playing track in your headphones and adjust by ear.
Watch out

Never go into the red. Clipping sounds harsh, can damage speakers, and makes the next track seem quiet.

Students can
  • Set trim correctly using the meter and their ears.
  • Keep the level even from one track to the next.
MR-K07

Genres at Main Room

Main Room widens the palette: the disco roots of club music, techno, tech house and R&B, plus two genres every student asks for.

GenreTypical BPMWhere and whenMixing it
Disco110-125New York and Philadelphia, 1970sLive drums drift: keep blends short or ride the tempo
Techno125-140Detroit 1980s, then BerlinLong, smooth blends shaped with EQ and filters
Tech house122-128UK and Europe, 1990sLong blends with a careful bass swap
R&B60-110US from the 1940s, modern R&B from the 1980sShort blends or cuts. Mind the vocals
Amapiano110-115South Africa, mid-2010sSwap the log drum bass carefully
Trap and UK drill130-150 (half-time feel)Atlanta 2000s, Chicago and London 2010sCount in half time and cut on the phrase
MR-K08

Disco

Disco was the first music made for DJs. Its long, groove-heavy records invented the club night and led directly to house.

Tempo
110-125 BPM
Born
New York and Philadelphia, early 1970s
Rhythm
Four to the floor, busy hi-hats
Sound
Strings, bass guitar, soaring vocals
Grew out of
Soul and funkMotownPhilly soulLatin percussion
Disco
Led to
HouseHi-NRGItalo discoNu-disco

Brief history

In the early 1970s, New York DJs such as David Mancuso at the Loft, and later Larry Levan at the Paradise Garage, played soul and funk records for dancers all night. Their crowds were mostly Black, Latino and gay, and the clubs welcomed people who weren't welcome elsewhere. In Philadelphia, the Philadelphia International label and its house band MFSB created the lush strings and four-to-the-floor drums that became the disco sound.

Producers responded with longer tracks built for the dancefloor. Remixer Tom Moulton helped invent the 12-inch single, which was louder and longer than a 7-inch and perfect for DJs. By 1977 disco was everywhere, from Studio 54 to the film Saturday Night Fever. Donna Summer and Giorgio Moroder's "I Feel Love" used synthesisers for almost everything and pointed towards electronic dance music.

A backlash in 1979 pushed disco out of the charts, but it survived in clubs and became house. Disco-pop is back today through artists such as Dua Lipa.

What to listen for

  • A four-to-the-floor kick with busy, open hi-hats on the offbeat.
  • Live bass guitar lines that bounce around the beat.
  • Strings, horns and piano playing big, joyful parts.
  • Soaring soul and gospel vocals.
  • Long extended mixes with instrumental breaks.

Artists who shaped it

DMDavid MancusoThe Loft, where the modern club night began
LLLarry LevanParadise Garage resident, legendary for his sound
TMTom MoultonInvented the extended remix and the 12-inch single
GMGiorgio MoroderBuilt the electronic disco sound
NRNile Rodgers and ChicFunky guitar and grooves sampled for decades
DSDonna Summer"The Queen of Disco"

Key artists now

PDPurple Disco MachineGerman producer of disco-house hits
HMHorse Meat DiscoLondon DJs keeping the original sound alive
DLDua LipaBrought disco-pop back to the top of the charts
Tunes that shaped it
  • MFSBTSOP (The Sound of Philadelphia) (1974)

Older disco was played by live drummers, so the tempo wanders. Keep blends short, or ride the tempo slider to keep tracks together.

  • Explain how disco led to house.

MR-K09

Techno

Techno is house's harder, more futuristic cousin: driving, repetitive and built from machines.

Tempo
125-140 BPM, faster today
Born
Detroit, mid-1980s
Rhythm
Relentless kick on every beat
Sound
Dark, hypnotic, industrial
Grew out of
Kraftwerk and synth-popElectro and funkChicago house
Techno
Led to
MinimalHard technoTranceTech house

Brief history

Three friends from Belleville, near Detroit, created techno: Juan Atkins, Derrick May and Kevin Saunderson. They mixed the funk they grew up with and the electronic music of the German group Kraftwerk, and imagined the future of a city whose car factories were closing. Atkins had already made electro as Cybotron, and the "Belleville Three" released records on their own labels.

In the 1990s, a second wave of Detroit artists, including Jeff Mills and the collective Underground Resistance, made techno harder and more political. When the Berlin Wall fell in 1989, techno became the sound of a reunited Berlin. Clubs such as Tresor opened in empty buildings, and Berlin became techno's second home. Today techno ranges from deep and hypnotic to fast hard techno at 150 BPM and above.

What to listen for

  • A kick on every beat that drives the track forward.
  • Machine sounds, especially the Roland TR-909.
  • Short loops that change slowly over many bars.
  • Few or no vocals.
  • A darker, more serious mood, often in minor keys.

Artists who shaped it

JAJuan Atkins"The originator", as Cybotron and Model 500
DMDerrick May"Strings of Life", as Rhythim Is Rhythim
KSKevin SaundersonTook techno into the charts with Inner City
JMJeff Mills"The Wizard", with lightning-fast mixing
URUnderground ResistanceDetroit collective that made it harder
RHRichie HawtinPioneered minimal techno as Plastikman

Key artists now

CDCharlotte de WitteBelgian DJ leading the dark, driving sound
ALAmelie LensBelgian DJ and label owner
ABAdam BeyerSwedish DJ behind the Drumcode label
SLSara LandryOne of the biggest names in hard techno
Tunes that shaped it
  • CybotronClear (1983)
  • Model 500No UFO's (1985)
  • Rhythim Is RhythimStrings of Life (1987)
  • Inner CityGood Life (1988)
  • Jeff MillsThe Bells (1997)
  • Adam Beyer & Bart SkilsYour Mind (2018)
Tutor tip

Techno is mixed in long blends, often several phrases, using EQ and filters to carve one track into the other. It's the best genre for practising MR-S01.

Students can
  • Explain where techno came from and how it reached Berlin.
  • Name the Belleville Three.
  • Make a long techno blend using EQ.
MR-K10

Tech house

Tech house takes house's groove and techno's stripped-back drive, and adds rolling basslines made for big rooms.

Tempo
122-128 BPM
Born
UK and Europe, 1990s
Rhythm
Four to the floor, lots of percussion
Sound
Heavy, bouncing bass, vocal hooks
Grew out of
HouseTechnoMinimal
Tech house
Led to
Bass houseBig-room festival sound

Brief history

Tech house grew in mid-1990s London, when DJs such as Terry Francis, Eddie Richards and Nathan Coles wanted something funkier than techno but tougher than house. Their club night Wiggle and venues such as The End helped define it.

In the 2000s and 2010s it exploded on Ibiza and the festival circuit. Mark Knight's label Toolroom and Jamie Jones and Lee Foss's Hot Creations made it one of the biggest sounds in club music. In 2018, Fisher's "Losing It" became a global hit and earned a Grammy nomination.

What to listen for

  • A punchy four-to-the-floor kick at 122-128 BPM.
  • Rolling, bouncing basslines that carry the whole track.
  • Lots of percussion: shakers, bongos, toms and claps.
  • Short, catchy vocal hooks rather than full songs.
  • Long, DJ-friendly intros and outros.

Artists who shaped it

TFTerry FrancisWiggle resident, one of the first tech house DJs
EREddie RichardsUK acid house veteran who helped define the sound
MKMark KnightFounded Toolroom Records in 2003
JJJamie JonesHot Creations co-founder and Ibiza star

Key artists now

FFisherAustralian producer behind "Losing It"
CLChris LakeUK producer and Black Book Records founder
JSJohn SummitUS DJ who sells out arenas
PTPatrick ToppingNewcastle DJ and Trick Records founder
Tunes that shaped it
  • Jamie JonesHungry for the Power
  • Patrick ToppingForget
  • FisherLosing It (2018)
  • Chris Lake & Alexis RobertsTurn Off the Lights (2018)
  • John Summit & HaylaWhere You Are (2023)
Tutor tip

Tech house basslines are the whole track. Never let two run together. Use a slow bass swap or a low-pass filter on the outgoing track.

Students can
  • Recognise tech house and explain how it differs from house and techno.
  • Name a pioneer and a current tech house artist.
  • Blend two tech house tracks without the basslines clashing.
MR-K11

R&B

R&B is soul, groove and vocals. It has shaped pop for 70 years, and today's R&B mixes it with hip hop production.

Tempo
60-110 BPM
Born
US, 1940s; modern R&B from the 1980s
Rhythm
Laid back, swung
Sound
Vocal-led, smooth, emotional
Grew out of
BluesGospelJazzSoul
R&B
Led to
New jack swingNeo-soulUK R&BAfroswing

Brief history

"Rhythm and blues" was the name the American music industry gave Black popular music in the late 1940s. It grew into soul through Ray Charles, Sam Cooke and Aretha Franklin, and labels such as Motown turned it into pop.

In the late 1980s, producer Teddy Riley created new jack swing by mixing R&B with hip hop beats. Mary J. Blige, TLC and Destiny's Child followed in the 1990s, then Usher and Beyoncé, and producers such as Timbaland and The Neptunes became stars in their own right. In the UK, Craig David, Ms. Dynamite and later Jorja Smith and Cleo Sol built a UK R&B sound, often linked with garage.

What to listen for

  • Vocals first: smooth melodies, harmonies and ad-libs.
  • Rich chords from keys, guitar and strings.
  • A relaxed, swung groove, often with hip hop drums.
  • Modern tracks use 808 bass and trap-style hi-hats.
  • Songs about love and relationships, usually 3-4 minutes long.

Artists who shaped it

RCRay CharlesMixed gospel and blues to help create soul
AFAretha Franklin"The Queen of Soul"
MGMarvin GayeTook R&B into deep, personal and political songs
TRTeddy RileyInvented new jack swing
MJMary J. Blige"The Queen of Hip Hop Soul"
CDCraig DavidLed UK R&B and garage around 2000

Key artists now

SSZAOne of the biggest R&B artists in the world
FOFrank OceanInfluential, experimental singer-songwriter
JSJorja SmithBRIT-winning Walsall singer
RRayeRecord-breaking BRIT Award winner
Tunes that shaped it
  • Ray CharlesWhat'd I Say (1959)
  • Aretha FranklinRespect (1967)
  • Marvin GayeWhat's Going On (1971)
  • BlackstreetNo Diggity (1996)
  • Destiny's ChildSay My Name (1999)
  • UsherYeah! (2004)
  • SZASnooze (2022)

Mixing R&B

  • Tempos vary a lot, so group tracks by speed before the set.
  • Tracks are short and vocal-heavy. Blend over intros and outros, or cut on the phrase.
  • Choose tracks for their mood and lyrics as well as their beat (see HL-K17).
Students can
  • Recognise R&B and name artists from two eras.
  • Mix R&B tracks without clashing vocals.
MR-K12

Amapiano

New

Amapiano is South Africa's biggest export: laid-back house grooves, jazzy keys and the deep, rolling log drum.

Tempo
110-115 BPM
Born
Gauteng, South Africa, mid-2010s
Rhythm
Steady kick, shuffled percussion
Sound
Log drum bass, piano, airy vocals
Grew out of
KwaitoDeep houseJazz and loungeBacardi house
Amapiano

Private school pianoAfrobeats crossovers

Brief history

Amapiano ("the pianos" in isiZulu) grew in the townships around Johannesburg and Pretoria in the mid-2010s. Young producers mixed deep house, jazz, lounge and kwaito, South Africa's own 1990s house sound, and shared tracks on WhatsApp and social media long before radio played them.

Its signature is the log drum, a booming, pitched percussive bass. Producers Kabza De Small and DJ Maphorisa, working together as Scorpion Kings, defined the sound. Focalistic's "Ke Star" became an anthem in 2020, Uncle Waffles' viral dancing DJ sets took it worldwide, and Tyla's "Water" won the first Grammy for Best African Music Performance in 2024.

What to listen for

  • A steady kick at 110-115 BPM with a relaxed, rolling feel.
  • The log drum: a deep, bouncing, pitched bass hit.
  • Shakers and shuffled percussion filling every gap.
  • Jazzy piano chords and soft synth pads.
  • Airy vocals, chants and spoken phrases, often in isiZulu, Sesotho or Setswana.

Artists who shaped it

KDKabza De Small"King of Amapiano", half of Scorpion Kings
MDJ MaphorisaProducer and the other half of Scorpion Kings
MSMFR SoulsEarly duo who helped define the sound
KMKelvin MomoPioneered the softer "private school piano" style
FFocalisticRapper behind the anthem "Ke Star"

Key artists now

UWUncle WafflesEswatini-born DJ who took it worldwide
TTylaGrammy-winning singer who took it to the charts
TITyler ICUProducer behind the hit "Mnike"
Tunes that shaped it

  • Kabza De Small & DJ MaphorisaSponono (2020)
  • Uncle WafflesTanzania (2022)

  • TylaWater (2023)

The log drum carries both bass and rhythm. Swap the low EQ cleanly, or the two log drums will fight. Amapiano tracks are long with gentle intros, which makes them good for long blends.

Students can
