MR-K13

Trap and UK drill

New

Trap and drill are the sound of modern rap: booming 808 bass, rattling hi-hats and a half-time feel.

Tempo
130-150 BPM, felt at half speed
Born
Atlanta 2000s; Chicago and London 2010s
Rhythm
Half-time drums, rolling hi-hats
Sound
808 bass, dark melodies
Grew out of
Southern hip hopCrunkChicago drillGrime and UK rap
Trap and drill
Led to
UK drillBrooklyn drillEDM trapJersey drill

Brief history

Trap began in Atlanta in the 2000s. T.I.'s 2003 album Trap Muzik named it, and artists such as Gucci Mane and Young Jeezy built it, using the Roland TR-808's booming bass and fast, rolling hi-hats. Producers such as Zaytoven and Lex Luger defined the beats, and by the 2010s Migos and Future had made trap the sound of mainstream rap.

Drill started in Chicago in the early 2010s with Chief Keef. In South London, groups such as 67 created UK drill, with sliding 808 basslines and a darker, faster bounce. In 2021, Russ Millions and Tion Wayne's "Body" became the first drill track to reach number one in the UK, and artists such as Central Cee took the sound global.

What to listen for

  • A half-time feel: 140 BPM that feels like 70.
  • Booming 808 bass, which slides between notes in UK drill.
  • Rolling hi-hats in triplets and fast bursts.
  • Dark, minor-key melodies on piano, strings or bells.
  • Rapped vocals, often with ad-libs.

Artists who shaped it

TT.I.Named trap with Trap Muzik
GMGucci ManeOne of trap's founding artists
ZZaytovenProducer who shaped the Atlanta trap sound
CKChief KeefStarted Chicago drill
667South London group who helped create UK drill
HOHeadie OneTook UK drill into the charts

Key artists now

CCCentral CeeUK drill's biggest global star
MBMetro BoominUS producer behind huge trap hits
TSTravis ScottTrap artist who sells out stadiums
Tunes that shaped it
  • T.I.What You Know (2006)
  • Chief KeefI Don't Like (2012)
  • MigosBad and Boujee (2016)
  • Headie One, AJ Tracey & StormzyAin't It Different (2020)
  • Russ Millions & Tion WayneBody (2021)
  • Central CeeDoja (2022)

Mixing trap and drill

  • Count in half time. At 140 BPM the music feels like 70. Phrases are usually 8 or 16 bars.
  • Cut, don't blend. Two 808 basslines sliding at once sound terrible.
  • Use the drops. Most tracks have a clear moment to cut into after the intro.
Watch out

Many trap and drill tracks contain explicit or violent lyrics. Use clean versions in school, check lyrics before a showcase, and agree what's suitable with the school.

Students can
  • Explain the half-time feel.
  • Name a trap pioneer and a UK drill artist.
  • Mix trap or drill tracks with clean cuts on the phrase.
MR-K14

Transients and quantise

Every drum hit starts with a sharp spike called a transient. Software uses transients to find the beat, and quantise uses that beat to snap your timing into place.

A transient is the very start of a sound: the attack. Drums have sharp transients, which is why they look like spikes on a waveform. When rekordbox analyses a track, it finds those spikes and places a beat grid on them.

Quantise snaps cue points, hot cues and loops to the nearest beat on the grid. Press a hot cue slightly late and quantise moves it onto the beat.

When to turn quantise off

  • When the beat grid is wrong (fix the grid first: MR-R02).
  • When you want to set a cue on something off the beat, such as a vocal pickup.
  • For hot cue drumming and some juggling routines, where you play rhythms between the beats.
Students can
  • Explain what a transient is and why it matters to rekordbox.
  • Turn quantise on and off and explain when to use each.
MR-K15

Harmonic blending

Harmonic blending means choosing tracks whose keys share most of their notes, so melodies and vocals sound good together.

The basics of harmony

There are 12 different notes, from C up to B. The gap between neighbouring notes is a semitone, and two semitones make a tone. A scale is a pattern of tones and semitones, and a key is the set of notes from one scale. C major uses only the white keys on a piano: C, D, E, F, G, A, B.

Keys that share most notes sound good together:

  • Relative major and minor: exactly the same notes. C major and A minor are relatives.
  • Dominant: the key five notes up (G major from C major). One note different.
  • Subdominant: the key four notes up (F major from C major). One note different.

The Camelot wheel

The Camelot wheel turns those relationships into numbers. Moving one number round the wheel is moving to the dominant or subdominant. Swapping A and B on the same number is moving to the relative major or minor.

Tutor tip

The circle of fifths is the same wheel musicians use, with key names instead of Camelot codes. Students taking GCSE Music may already know it, so make the link for them.

When key matters

Key matters most when melodies, chords or vocals overlap. Drum-only intros and outros are forgiving. A good rule: check key whenever both tracks will have melody playing at once.

Students can
  • Explain relative, dominant and subdominant keys.
  • Use the Camelot wheel to pick compatible tracks.
  • Hear the difference between a harmonic and a clashing blend.
MR-K16

Improvisation: reading the room

A good DJ watches the crowd as much as the decks, and changes the plan when the room asks for it.

What you seeWhat it meansTry
Singing and hands upIt's workingStay in the same lane: same artist, label, genre or era
A full floor, people joiningEnergy is buildingKeep building, or hold here
People leaving the floorLosing themA track everyone knows, or a change of genre
Chatting, not dancingLow engagementMore energy, or a bigger, more familiar tune
People taking breaksTiredA few lower-energy tracks, then build back up
Game

Crowd Cards. Flip a card such as "the floor's emptying" or "they want a classic". The student chooses the next track and explains why.

Students can
  • Describe signs that a crowd is enjoying a set or losing interest.
  • Change the plan sensibly in response to a crowd card.
MR-K17

Structuring a mix: genre and energy

Main Room students plan sets two ways: grouping tracks by genre, and shaping energy across the whole set.

By genre

Group tracks of the same genre together and move through the genres in an order that makes sense for tempo and energy. In a 60-minute set, that might be four or five blocks of about 12 minutes.

By energy

Some DJs build steadily. Some ride a rollercoaster of build-ups and breakdowns. Some mix drop to drop to keep energy high. A warm-up set should leave room for the next DJ, so it shouldn't peak too early.

Students can
  • Plan a set grouped by genre in a sensible order.
  • Draw the energy shape of a planned set and explain it.
Main Room

Skills

MR-S01

Filters

A filter removes everything above or below a point. It's the smoothest way to bring a track in or out, and it builds tension like nothing else.

A high-pass filter lets high frequencies through and removes the lows. A low-pass filter does the opposite. Most controllers put both on one knob: turn right for high-pass, left for low-pass, and the middle is off.

Using filters

  • Bring a track in with the high-pass filter on, then slowly open it.
  • Take a track out by sweeping the high-pass filter up, or the low-pass filter down.
  • Build tension by sweeping a high-pass filter up before a drop.
  • Balance a blend by filtering one track so the two don't crowd each other.
Tutor tip

Filters don't boost, they only cut. Return the knob to the middle after every transition, or the next mix starts wrong.

Students can
  • Use a high-pass and a low-pass filter in a blend.
  • Build tension with a filter sweep before a drop.
MR-S02

Looping

A loop repeats a section of a track. Use one to extend an outro when the next track needs more time, or to rescue a mix.

A good loop:

  • Starts on beat 1, ideally at the start of a phrase.
  • Lasts a whole number of bars, ideally a whole phrase (4, 8 or 16 bars).
  • Captures a complete musical idea and doesn't cut off a vocal or melody.

Outros are easiest to loop because they're usually just drums. Use quantise so the loop locks to the beat. Keep listening: if the grid is slightly off, the loop can slowly drift out of time with the other track.

Game

Loop Rescue. The outgoing track is about to end and the next one isn't ready. The student loops the outro to save the mix.

Students can
  • Set a clean loop on a phrase and exit it on the beat.
  • Use a loop to extend an outro during a blend.
MR-S03

Flare: the spinback

The spinback stops a track with a dramatic backwards spin. It comes from Jamaican sound system culture, where DJs spun a tune back to restart it when the crowd demanded.

To perform it, push the jog wheel or record hard anticlockwise so the track spins backwards and slows to a stop.

Drop in with a spinback

  1. Play deck A. Cue deck B on a strong point, such as a drop.
  2. In the last bar before the phrase change, spin deck A back.
  3. On the one, start deck B and switch the crossfader from A to B in the same moment.
Watch out

Use spinbacks sparingly. One at the right moment gets a cheer. Five in a set gets old.

Students can
  • Perform a clean spinback.
  • Drop the next track in on the one straight after a spinback.
MR-S04

Flare: scratching a track in

Scratching the first beat of the incoming track over the outgoing one is a classic hip hop way to bring a track in with style.

  1. Play deck A. Cue deck B on its first beat, with its hot cue set there.
  2. Move the crossfader to the middle so both decks can be heard.
  3. As the phrase change approaches, baby scratch deck B's first beat in time with deck A.
  4. On the one, let deck B go and snap the crossfader across to B.
Tutor tip

Keep the scratches short and rhythmic. The idea is to tease the next track, not cover the outgoing one.

Students can
  • Scratch a track in over another and release it on the one.
MR-S05

Flare: beat repeat and slip

Beat repeat stutters a tiny loop for a moment. With slip on, the track carries on silently underneath, so when you let go it's still in time.

Turn on slip, then hold a short loop or a beat repeat pad (such as a half or quarter beat). The sound stutters. When you let go, the track jumps to where it would have been if you'd never touched it.

Using beat repeat in a blend

  1. Bring the new track in, beatmatched, with its low EQ cut.
  2. In the bar before a phrase change, hold beat repeat for movement and tension.
  3. Let go on the one and swap the bass.
  4. Fade the old track out.
Watch out

Beat repeat is easy to overuse. Less is more: a single bar before a big moment is enough.

Students can
  • Use beat repeat with slip and stay in time.
MR-S06

Beatmatching by ear

At Main Room, students match tempo using only their ears: no BPM display, no sync.

The tempo slider changes speed as a percentage. At 120 BPM, moving it 2% adds 2.4 BPM. Once two tracks are lined up, the time it takes them to drift apart tells you how far out the tempo is: fast drift means a big gap, slow drift means a small one.

The ear-only routine

  1. Play deck A. Cover the BPM displays.
  2. Start deck B on the one, at the start of a phrase, and line it up with the jog wheel.
  3. Listen: is B running ahead or falling behind? How quickly?
  4. Move B's tempo about 1% in the right direction. Line up again.
  5. Still drifting? Make a smaller move. Repeat until it holds for a whole phrase.
Game

Screen Off. Tape over the displays and beatmatch two tracks of unknown tempo. Time how long it takes.

Students can
  • Match the tempo of two tracks by ear, without the display.
  • Keep them in time for a full phrase.
MR-S07

Transitions: going further

Main Room adds longer blends and faster, punchier changes. The skill is choosing the right one for the tracks.

Longer blends

Drop in

Like a straight cut, but you press PLAY on the new track and switch the crossfader in the same moment, usually right on a drop.

Drop in with a quick fade

Drop the new track in at the start of a phrase using its channel fader, then pull the old track's fader down quickly over a beat or two. It's softer than a straight cut.

Crossfader blend

A one-phrase blend done on the crossfader instead of the channel faders, with a bass swap in the middle. It's useful on setups where the faders are awkward to reach.

Tutor tip

Before each transition, ask the student to name it and say why it suits these two tracks. That's the real Main Room skill.

Students can
  • Perform three- and six-phrase blends.
  • Perform a drop in, a quick fade and a crossfader blend.
  • Choose and justify a transition for two given tracks.
MR-S08

Stab scratch

The stab is a very fast forward cut: a short, sharp burst of sound on the push, with the fader closed on the way back.

Push the sound forward quickly with the fader open, close the fader, then pull back. The difference from the forward cut is speed: a stab is a quick jab, so you hear a short, punchy hit.

Students can
  • Perform stabs in time on every beat, then on every half beat.
MR-S09

Tear scratch

The tear splits one movement into two, with a tiny pause in the middle, so a single push makes two sounds.

The fader stays open. Push forward, pause for a split second, push again. Then pull back the same way. Each stroke makes two sounds, so a forward and back makes four.

Teach it
  1. Practise the pause slowly, saying "ah-ah" for each half.
  2. Speed up while keeping the halves even.
Students can
  • Perform tears in time, with even halves.
MR-S10

Scribble scratch

The scribble is a fast, tight buzz made by tensing the forearm so the hand vibrates over the start of the sound.

The fader stays open. Keep the movement tiny and fast, close to 9 o'clock on the jog wheel. It sounds harsh on its own, so it works best as a short burst within a routine, or at the end of a phrase.

Students can
  • Perform a controlled scribble for one beat, then return to a baby scratch.
MR-S11

Chirp scratch

The chirp sounds like a bird. The fader closes during each stroke, so you only hear the start of every movement.

Do a baby scratch while the fader hand closes on the push and opens on the pull. Both hands move together, so it takes practice to coordinate. It's the first scratch where the jog wheel and crossfader work at the same time, which is why it sits at Main Room after students are confident with the baby scratch and forward cut.

Chirp combinations

Once the chirp is solid, combine it with other scratches over a one-bar loop:

  • Two baby scratches, then two chirps.
  • Chirp, chirp, stab, stab.
  • A tear followed by two chirps.
Game

Scratch Copycat. You play a one-bar pattern. The student copies it. Then swap roles.

Teach it
  1. Practise the fader movement on its own first, without the jog wheel.
  2. Add the jog wheel at half speed. Count out loud.
  3. Build up to full speed while keeping both hands in time.
Students can
  • Perform a slow chirp in time, then at full speed.
  • Play a one-bar pattern that combines at least two scratches.
MR-S12

Beat juggling: kick and snare drops

Set hot cues on single kick and snare hits, then play them like drum pads over another track to add your own rhythm.

Find an isolated kick and an isolated snare or clap in a track, and set a hot cue on each. Then trigger them over the playing track.

  1. Load the same track on both decks to begin with.
  2. Set hot cues on deck B: one on a lone kick, one on a lone snare.
  3. Play deck A. Use the hot cue pads and crossfader to drop deck B's kicks and snares in where they already fall.
  4. Then drop them in new places to create a fresh rhythm.
  5. Finally, use sounds from a different track.
Students can
  • Trigger kick and snare hot cues in time over a playing track.
  • Create a simple new rhythm with them.
MR-S13

Tap pausing

Tap pausing touches the jog wheel to pause the track for a moment, over and over, so the beat stutters and feels slower.

Each beat still plays at its normal speed, but the tiny pauses between them stretch the groove. Practised at a steady rhythm, it can make a 90 BPM beat feel noticeably slower.

Teach it
  1. Start with a slow track (80-90 BPM) and pause every two beats.
  2. Speed up the pattern as the student gets more accurate.
  3. Use a metronome to keep the pauses even.
Students can
  • Tap pause in a steady, repeatable pattern.
MR-S14

Doubling

Doubling plays two copies of the same track half a beat apart and flicks between them, doubling up the rhythm.

Beatmatch two copies of a track so deck B is exactly half a beat behind deck A. Then flick the crossfader from side to side every half beat. Because you hear each deck's beats on alternate halves, every beat appears twice.

In the lesson

In lessons we use Glue for doubling. Load it on both decks before the lesson so the student starts straight away.

Students can
  • Offset two copies by half a beat.
  • Switch between them in time for a full bar.
Main Room

rekordbox

MR-R01

Music management: going further

A Main Room library is organised so the right track is always seconds away, whatever the set needs.

Folders and playlists

  • By genre: a folder per genre, with playlists inside.
  • By event: a folder for each recurring event, such as a school showcase.
  • By position in a set: playlists named "Warm-up", "Build", "Peak", or energy 1 to 5.

Sorting tracks

  • Alphabetical: for finding a specific track quickly.
  • Set order: the order you plan to play them.
  • BPM: groups similar genres together in mixed playlists.
  • Key: shows your harmonic options at a glance.

Extra information

  • My Tag: your own labels, such as "dark", "vocal" or "crowd-pleaser".
  • Comments: notes about structure, such as "long intro" or "drop at 1:05".
  • Rating and colour: use them for energy or set position. Keep your own system consistent.
Students can
  • Organise a library by genre and by set position.
  • Sort a playlist by BPM and key, and add tags or comments.
MR-R02

Changing beat grids

rekordbox usually places the beat grid correctly, but not always. A wrong grid breaks quantise, loops and sync, so every track should be checked before a set.

Fixing a grid

  1. Zoom in on the first kick. Is the grid line on its front edge?
  2. Open grid edit mode.
  3. Shift the whole grid left or right until it sits on the kick.
  4. Set the bar's first beat so bar and phrase markers line up with the music.
  5. Play through the track and check the grid stays on the kicks to the end.
  6. If it drifts partway through, reset the grid from the first wrong beat.
Tutor tip

Use the metronome in grid edit mode. If the click and the kick flam (sound like two hits), the grid is off.

Students can
  • Spot an incorrect beat grid and fix it.
  • Set the first beat of the bar correctly.
MR-R03

Structural markers

Marking a track's sections before a set shows the structure at a glance and makes every transition easier.

Use memory cues or hot cues as markers. Many DJs keep a simple system, such as:

Newer versions of rekordbox can also analyse a track's phrases and colour them on the waveform. Use it as a guide, but check by ear.

Tutor tip

Ask students to choose one marking system and use it on every track. A consistent system means they can read any track instantly.

Students can
  • Mark the sections of a track with cues before a set.
MR-R04

Hot cues, memory cues and loops

rekordbox has four ways to save points in a track. Each does a different job.

FeatureWhat it doesUse it for
Hot cueJumps straight to a point and plays from itPerformance: drops, vocal hooks, juggling
Memory cueMarks a point. Jumping to it doesn't start playbackMarkers: intro, breakdown, mix-out point
Saved loopStores a loop of a set length on a hot cue or memory cueLoops you'll use every time, such as a clean outro loop
Active loopA saved loop that switches on automatically when playback reaches itMaking sure the outro never runs out
  1. Load a track and move to the point you want.
  2. Set a hot cue from the performance pads, or press memory to save a memory cue.
  3. To save a loop, set the loop first, then save it to a hot cue or memory cue.
  4. To make a saved loop active, switch on its active setting in the memory list.
Students can
  • Set and use hot cues and memory cues.
  • Save a loop and make it active.
MR-R05

rekordbox settings

Knowing the settings means students can fix problems and set rekordbox up the way they work.

AreaWhat it controlsWhy it matters
ViewLayout, waveform colours, what shows on screenA clearer screen for each student
AudioOutput device, sample rate, buffer sizeFixes no sound, crackles or delays
AnalysisBPM range, key detection, analysis modeBetter BPM and beat grid results
ControllerDeck, mixer, FX and sampler settingsHow the controller behaves
RecordingWhere recorded mixes are savedFinding recordings afterwards
Tutor tip

If a student hears crackles, increase the buffer size. If there's a delay between pressing a button and hearing it, decrease it.

Students can
  • Find the audio, analysis and recording settings.
  • Fix a basic sound problem using the settings.
MR-R06

The harmonic traffic light

rekordbox can highlight tracks whose key works with the track you're playing, so harmonic choices take seconds.

With the feature switched on, rekordbox compares each track in your collection with the master deck and highlights the ones in compatible keys, usually in green. It turns MR-K15 into a quick visual check during a set.

  1. Load and play a track so it's the master deck.
  2. Turn on key matching in the browser (the switch's name and position depend on the rekordbox version).
  3. Look for highlighted tracks in your collection or playlist.
  4. Preview one in your headphones before you commit.
Watch out

The highlight is a guide, not a rule. Software sometimes detects the wrong key. Always check by ear.

Students can
  • Switch on key matching and use it to choose a compatible track.
Stage 3 of 3 · 27 topics

The Headliner

Confident DJs develop their own style: effects with control, acapellas, big jumps in tempo, scratch and hot cue routines, and sets that tell a story. They finish by performing to a real audience.

Level-up check

A 15-20 minute set with a planned journey, including at least one major tempo or genre change and one creative technique (stems, acapella, routine or scratching). Effects must be used with control. Where possible, it's performed at a showcase or to the class. Afterwards the student explains one choice they're proud of and one thing they'd change.

Headliner

Knowledge

HL-K01

The machines behind the music

A handful of drum machines, synthesisers and samplers shaped almost every genre in this handbook. Headliners should know them by sound and by name.

Minimoog (1970)A portable, reliable synth that put synthesisers on stage. Warm, powerful bass and leads, one note at a time.
Roland TR-808 (1980)Flopped at first, then defined electro, hip hop and trap. Its booming kick is everywhere today.
Roland TR-909 (1983)Punchy kicks and crisp claps. The sound of early house and techno.
Yamaha DX7 (1983)One of the first hit digital synths. Bright, glassy tones that defined 1980s pop.
E-mu SP-1200 (1987)A gritty 12-bit drum machine and sampler at the heart of golden-era hip hop.
Akai MPC (1988 on)Pads for chopping and playing samples. Still the image of the hip hop producer.
Software (1990s on)Ableton Live, FL Studio and Logic put the whole studio on a laptop.

Hear them in the music

  • The 808 kick and cowbell on Afrika Bambaataa & the Soulsonic Force's "Planet Rock" and Marvin Gaye's "Sexual Healing".
  • The 808 bass that drives almost every trap and drill track.
  • The 909 hats and claps under classic Chicago house and Detroit techno.
Game

Name That Machine. Play short examples of an 808 kick, a 909 clap and a sampled break. The student names the source.

Students can
  • Name the main classic machines and the genres they shaped.
  • Recognise an 808 kick and a 909 clap by ear.
HL-K02

Pulse: anything in the track

Headliners can lock onto any part of a track, not just the kick, and answer questions about its structure without looking.

Students should clap along to:

  • The kick in a grime or drum and bass track, where it doesn't fall on every beat.
  • The hi-hats or snare in a house track.
  • The rhythm of a bassline or melody.

And answer questions such as:

  • On which beats does the crash cymbal play?
  • In which bar does the cowbell first appear?
  • How many bars long is the repeating kick pattern?
Students can
  • Clap along to any rhythmic part of a track.
  • Answer structure questions by ear, without the waveform.
HL-K03

Signal flow: effects

Where an effect sits in the signal path decides what the channel fader does to it. That's the difference between an echo that stops dead and one that rings out.

  • Pre-fader effects (filter and colour FX) come before the channel fader. Close the fader and the effect disappears with the music.
  • Post-fader effects (most beat FX: echo, delay, reverb) come after it. Close the fader and the effect's tail keeps ringing out. That's why an echo can carry on after a track has gone.
  • Send and return route the sound out to an external effects unit and back into the mixer.
Students can
  • Explain pre-fader and post-fader effects.
  • Use a post-fader echo to leave a tail after cutting a track.
HL-K04

Equipment functions: crossfader and FX

Headliners set the mixer up for what they're about to do, from scratching to effects-heavy mixing.

Crossfader settings

  • Assign: each channel can be set to the crossfader's left side, right side, or through (it ignores the crossfader).
  • Curve: smooth for blending, sharp for scratching (see MR-K05).

FX controls

ControlWhat it does
FX selectChooses the effect
Channel selectChooses which channel, or the master, gets the effect
Beat valueSets the effect's timing, such as 1/2, 1 or 2 beats
Level/depth (dry/wet)How much effect is mixed in. Fully dry is no effect, fully wet is only effect
On/offSwitches the effect in and out
Students can
  • Set the crossfader assign and curve for a scratch routine.
  • Choose, time and apply an effect to the right channel.
HL-K05

Levels: when tracks don't match

Not all tracks are equally loud, and not all equipment sends the same level. Headliners balance a set by ear, not just by the meters.

  • Older tracks were often mastered quieter than modern ones, so a 1990s classic can sound weak after a 2025 track.
  • File quality: a low-quality MP3 has less impact than a WAV, even at the same meter level.
  • Different sources: a turntable, a media player and a drum machine all send different levels into the mixer.
  • Different genres: a bass-heavy track can read lower on the meter but feel louder.
Tutor tip

When switching between very different tracks, compare them in the headphones before the blend and match how loud they feel, not just the meters.

Students can
  • Balance tracks of different eras and genres so the set sounds even.
HL-K06

Headliner genres are faster, more complex and harder to mix. Several were born in the UK.

HL-K07

Trance

Trance is built for euphoria: long breakdowns, huge melodies and a build that seems to go on forever.

Tempo
130-140 BPM
Born
Germany and Goa, early 1990s
Rhythm
Four to the floor, rolling offbeat bass
Sound
Uplifting chords, big melodies, long breakdowns
Grew out of
TechnoAcid houseSynth-popGoa psychedelic parties
Trance
Led to
ProgressiveUpliftingPsytranceHard tranceEDM

Brief history

Trance grew from techno and acid house in Frankfurt in the early 1990s, where DJs such as Sven Väth and labels such as Eye Q built a hypnotic, melodic sound. At the same time, all-night beach parties in Goa, India, created psychedelic Goa trance, which later became psytrance.

By the late 1990s trance was the biggest club sound in Europe. In the UK, superclubs such as Gatecrasher in Sheffield and Cream in Liverpool packed out every weekend, and tracks such as Robert Miles' "Children", ATB's "9 PM (Till I Come)" and Darude's "Sandstorm" filled the charts. Dutch DJs Tiësto and Armin van Buuren became global stars. Tiësto played at the opening ceremony of the 2004 Athens Olympics, and Armin's radio show A State of Trance has run weekly since 2001. Trance's big breakdowns and builds later shaped EDM.

What to listen for

  • A four-to-the-floor kick at 130-140 BPM with a rolling offbeat bassline.
  • Long breakdowns where the drums drop out completely.
  • Huge build-ups with snare rolls and rising synths.
  • Big arpeggios and wide, layered "supersaw" chords.
  • Emotional, euphoric melodies, often in minor keys but uplifting.

Artists who shaped it

SVSven VäthFrankfurt DJ and label boss at the start of it all
PVPaul van DykBerlin DJ behind "For an Angel"
SJSasha and John DigweedUK DJs who shaped progressive trance
FCFerry CorstenDutch producer behind huge late-1990s hits
TTiëstoThe first trance DJ to become a global superstar
AVArmin van BuurenHost of A State of Trance

Key artists now

AVArmin van BuurenStill one of the biggest names in trance
ABAbove & BeyondUK trio known for emotional, singalong sets
TTiëstoMoved into EDM and pop, still headlining festivals
Tunes that shaped it

Tutor tip

Trance breakdowns can last a minute or more. Mix in the intro or the outro, never across a breakdown, and always mix in compatible keys: the melodies are the whole point.

HL-K08

Drum and bass and jungle

Drum and bass is Britain's fastest dance music: chopped breakbeats at 170 BPM over deep sub bass.

Tempo
160-176 BPM
Born
London and the UK, early 1990s
Rhythm
Fast, broken breakbeats
Sound
Heavy sub bass, chopped breaks
Grew out of
Breakbeat hardcoreReggae and dancehallHip hop breaksTechno
JungleDrum and bass
Led to
LiquidNeurofunkJump upDubstep

Brief history

Jungle came out of the UK rave scene in the early 1990s. Producers sped up sampled drum breaks, especially the "Amen break" from the Winstons' 1969 B-side "Amen, Brother", and added reggae and dancehall bass, vocals and MCs. Pirate radio spread it across London, and club nights such as Fabio and Grooverider's Rage at Heaven became its home.

As the sound grew cleaner and more technical, it became drum and bass. Goldie's "Inner City Life" and Roni Size and Reprazent's Mercury Prize win in 1997 took it to new audiences. LTJ Bukem's Good Looking label created the smooth, atmospheric style later called liquid, while labels such as Metalheadz, Ram Records and Hospital Records built the scene. In the 2020s drum and bass and jungle are back in the charts and at festivals, led by a new generation such as Nia Archives.

What to listen for

  • A fast tempo of 160-176 BPM.
  • Chopped breakbeats such as the Amen break, or a tight "two-step" beat.
  • Deep sub bass you feel more than hear, plus heavy mid-range bass in some styles.
  • In jungle: reggae basslines, dancehall vocals and MCs.
  • Long 16- and 32-bar phrases that build towards big drops.

Artists who shaped it

GGoldieMetalheadz founder, "Inner City Life"
FGFabio and GrooveriderRage DJs and Radio 1 pioneers
LBLTJ BukemCreated the smooth, liquid sound
RSRoni SizeMercury Prize winner with Reprazent
ACAndy CRam Records boss, famous for fast mixing and double drops
SFShy FX"Original Nuttah", a jungle classic

Key artists now

CSChase & StatusDuo behind "Baddadan" and BRIT Producers of the Year
NANia ArchivesLeader of the jungle revival
SFSub FocusFestival headliner and producer
HHedexOne of the most-booked DJs in jump up
Tunes that shaped it

Mixing drum and bass

  • Count in 16 and 32 bars. Intros are long, so blends can be too.
  • Double drops: line up two tracks so both drops hit at the same moment. It's the genre's signature move, and needs perfect phrasing.
  • Rewinds are part of the culture, as in grime.
Students can
  • Explain the roots of jungle and drum and bass.
  • Name two pioneers and two current artists.
  • Perform a double drop.
HL-K09

Dubstep

Dubstep slowed the feel down to half time and turned the bass up. It began in South London and went global.

Tempo
138-142 BPM, felt at half speed
Born
Croydon and South London, early 2000s
Rhythm
Half-time, snare on beat 3
Sound
Deep sub bass, space, wobble
Grew out of
UK garage and 2-stepDub and reggaeJungleGrime
Dubstep
Led to
BrostepRiddimFuture garage

Brief history

Dubstep grew from the darker side of UK garage and from dub reggae around Croydon in the early 2000s. The Big Apple Records shop was a meeting point, and producers such as Skream, Benga and Digital Mystikz (Mala and Coki) built the sound. The club night FWD>> in London and the DMZ nights in Brixton were its home, and pirate radio station Rinse FM spread it.

In 2006, Mary Anne Hobbs' "Dubstep Warz" show on BBC Radio 1 introduced it to a national audience. Burial's moody albums showed how emotional it could be, and Magnetic Man took it into the top 10. In the 2010s a louder, more aggressive US style led by Skrillex filled arenas.

What to listen for

  • A tempo of about 140 BPM with a half-time feel: the snare lands on beat 3.
  • Deep, rumbling sub bass, often with a "wobble" that pulses in time.
  • Lots of space and dub-style echoes in the original UK sound.
  • Dark, heavy atmospheres.
  • In US-style dubstep: aggressive, growling mid-range bass and big drops.

Artists who shaped it

Key artists now

HL-K10

Breakbeat

Breakbeat uses broken, syncopated drum patterns instead of a steady kick on every beat. It links hip hop, rave, big beat and drum and bass.

Tempo
125-135 BPM
Born
Hip hop breaks, then UK rave
Rhythm
Broken and syncopated
Sound
Chopped drums, effects, big bass
Grew out of
Funk drum breaksHip hopAcid houseElectro
Breakbeat
Led to
Big beatNu skool breaksJungleBreaks-influenced UK bass

Brief history

Breakbeat comes from the same drum breaks hip hop DJs looped in the 1970s, especially funk records by James Brown and his drummers, such as Clyde Stubblefield on "Funky Drummer". In the UK rave scene of the late 1980s and early 1990s, producers sped those breaks up, chopped them and layered them under acid and rave synths. That "breakbeat hardcore" sound led to jungle.

In the late 1990s, big beat acts such as the Chemical Brothers, Fatboy Slim and the Prodigy took breakbeat into the charts and onto festival main stages. In the 2000s, nu skool breaks artists such as Stanton Warriors and Plump DJs kept it going in clubs. Breaks are back everywhere today, in UK garage, jungle revival and the work of acts such as Overmono and Bicep.

What to listen for

  • Broken, syncopated drum patterns rather than a kick on every beat.
  • Chopped classic breaks such as the Amen, "Funky Drummer" and "Think".
  • A snare on beats 2 and 4 holding everything together.
  • Big basslines, filters and effects.
  • In big beat: rock energy, samples and huge drops.

Artists who shaped it

CSClyde StubblefieldJames Brown's drummer, one of the most sampled beats ever

CBThe Chemical BrothersBig beat pioneers from Manchester

SWStanton WarriorsKept breaks alive in 2000s clubs

Key artists now

SWStanton WarriorsStill touring and releasing breaks

HL-K11

UK garage, 2-step and bassline

UK garage took American house, sped it up and gave it a skipping, swung groove. It sound-tracked London at the turn of the century and is back today.

Tempo
130-140 BPM
Born
London, mid-1990s
Rhythm
Swung, skipping 2-step drums
Sound
Chopped vocals, rolling bass
Grew out of
US garage and houseJungleR&B and soul vocalsDancehall
UK garage
Led to
2-stepSpeed garageGrimeDubstepBassline

Brief history

Garage started with soulful US house from New York and New Jersey (the name comes from the Paradise Garage club). American producer Todd Edwards' chopped vocal style was especially influential. London DJs played it faster at Sunday after-parties with MCs, and a UK sound emerged.

Speed garage added heavy bass. 2-step removed kicks for a skipping groove: MJ Cole's "Sincere" and Artful Dodger and Craig David's "Re-Rewind". Pirate radio and clubs such as Twice as Nice made it huge, and So Solid Crew's "21 Seconds" reached number one in 2001. Its darker side led to grime and dubstep.

In the mid-2000s, bassline grew from the same roots in Sheffield and the north of England, with wobbling basslines and a bouncier swing. Today a new generation has revived UK garage, and Interplanetary Criminal and Eliza Rose's "B.O.T.A." reached number one in 2022.

What to listen for

  • A tempo of 130-140 BPM with a strong swing.
  • 2-step drums: kicks missing from beats 2 and 4, so the beat skips.
  • Chopped, pitched-up vocal samples.
  • Rolling or wobbling basslines.
  • Smooth R&B vocals, often with an MC.

Afro house

Afro house blends deep house with African percussion, chants and melodies. It's one of the fastest-growing sounds in clubs.

Brief history

Afro house grew in South Africa in the 2000s, where deep house had become the country's favourite dance music. Producers added African percussion, chants and melodies, and the local style kwaito, to create a deeper, more spiritual sound.

Black Coffee became its biggest name. He took the sound from Durban to Ibiza residencies and global festivals, and won a Grammy in 2022. In the 2020s, European acts such as the Berlin collective Keinemusik made Afro-influenced house one of the biggest club sounds in the world.

What to listen for

  • A four-to-the-floor kick at 118-124 BPM.
  • Layers of hand percussion: congas, shakers and talking drums.
  • Chants, call-and-response vocals and African languages.
  • Deep, hypnotic grooves that build slowly.
  • Warm, melodic pads and synths.

Jersey club

New

Jersey club is fast and bouncy, built on a distinctive kick pattern and chopped vocal samples. It went viral on social media in the 2020s.

Brief history

Jersey club grew from Baltimore club music in Newark, New Jersey, in the early 2000s. DJs such as DJ Tameil brought the Baltimore sound to Newark, and local producers built tracks around a quick-fire kick pattern and short vocal chops, often remixing pop and R&B hits.

Its remixes spread on SoundCloud and later TikTok, where its bouncy rhythm suited dance challenges. By the 2020s it had shaped mainstream songs such as Lil Uzi Vert's "Just Wanna Rock" and NewJeans' "Super Shy", and Jersey drill mixed it with drill.

What to listen for

  • A tempo of 130-145 BPM.
  • The signature kick pattern: a rapid burst of kicks that makes the beat bounce.
  • Chopped vocal samples, often repeated in short bursts.
  • Sound effects such as the famous "bed squeak".
  • Short, high-energy tracks and remixes of songs people know.

HL-K14

Transition tracks

A transition track changes tempo or genre partway through. It does the hard work of a big tempo jump for you.

Some tracks start at one tempo and end at another, either with a sudden jump or a gradual ramp. Played at the right moment, they move a set from, say, 140 BPM to 170 BPM without any awkward mixing.

  1. Learn exactly where and how the tempo changes before you play the track.
  2. Mix the transition track in at its starting tempo.
  3. Finish mixing out the previous track before the change starts.
  4. Let the transition track change on its own. Don't mix over it.
  5. Mix the next track in at the new tempo.

Analysing transition tracks

rekordbox usually analyses only one tempo per track. To capture a tempo change, use the dynamic analysis mode in the analysis settings. It can make normal tracks less accurate, so keep transition tracks in their own playlist and only analyse them that way.

Students can
  • Use a transition track to move between two tempos.
  • Analyse a transition track correctly in rekordbox.
HL-K15

Acapellas

An acapella is a vocal with no music. Laid over an instrumental, it creates a mash-up only you can play.

Before using an acapella in a set, prepare it properly:

  • Tempo: without drums, software often gets the BPM wrong. Check it against the original track and save the right value.
  • Key: sung vocals have a key. Mix them over instrumentals in a compatible key, or they'll sound out of tune.
  • Level: vocals on their own can be much quieter or louder than full tracks. Set the trim so the mash-up sounds like one record.
  • Cue point: many vocals start just before beat 1 with a pickup note. Set the cue so the phrase lines up, not just the first sound.

Students can find official acapellas from labels and DJ stores, or create them with stem separation (HL-R02).

Students can
  • Prepare an acapella with the right tempo, key and cue point.
HL-K16

Improvisation: routines on the fly

Headliners can improvise scratch and juggling routines live, responding to the music and the crowd.

A good improvised routine balances repetition (catchy, simple ideas the crowd can follow) and variation (new ideas and more complex techniques). It also rises and falls in intensity: start musical and simple, build to a technical climax, then release.

  • Respond to the music: drop-cut a spoken word so it adds to the lyrics, or juggle in the same rhythm as the track.
  • Use simple forms: patterns such as AABA give a routine shape.
  • Read the reaction: repeat what gets a response, and move on from what doesn't.
  • Keep within your limits: precision is harder without preparation, especially on stage.
Students can
  • Improvise a short routine with a clear shape.
  • Adapt a routine in response to the crowd.
HL-K17

Structuring a mix: vibe and story

Headliners build sets with a narrative. The tracks connect technically and through their mood and message.

By vibe

Even within one genre, sections of a set can feel very different. For example, in a drum and bass set: crowd-pleasing anthems to get people moving, old-school jungle as a nod to the roots, heavy tracks for the peak, then liquid drum and bass to wind down.

By emotion and message

Group tracks by what they say as well as how they sound. An R&B set might move from singalong ballads to love songs, then party tracks, then a final singalong. The lyrics carry the crowd from one feeling to the next.

Tutor tip

Ask students to give their showcase set a title and three chapters. If they can't describe the story, the set doesn't have one yet.

Students can
  • Plan a set structured by vibe or emotion and explain the story.
Headliner

Skills

HL-S01

Effects

Effects add texture and drama. Used with control, they lift a set. Used all the time, they bury the music.

EffectWhat it doesUse it to
EchoRepeats the sound, fading each timeAdd a tail to a cut or spinback, fill a quiet moment
DelayPlays the sound back after a set number of beatsCreate movement, lift a build-up, play with rhythm
ReverbAdds the sound of a big spaceMake a breakdown or acapella feel huge, add a tail
FlangerA sweeping, jet-like swooshEnhance a build-up or a pad in a breakdown
RollRepeats a tiny slice (like beat repeat)Build tension before a drop
  1. Choose the effect and the channel.
  2. Set the beat value to suit the tempo and the moment.
  3. Switch it on and bring in the level.
  4. Bring the level back down, then switch it off cleanly on the beat.

Examples

  • Echo out: switch on echo just before a quick fade, so the outgoing track rings out after it's gone.
  • Delay into a swap: trigger a delay on the outgoing track just before the bass swap in a blend.
  • Reverb tail: add reverb as you make a straight cut, so the cut feels deliberate rather than abrupt.
Watch out

One effect per transition is plenty. If you can't say why an effect is on, switch it off.

Students can
  • Use echo, delay, reverb and flanger with control.
  • Switch effects on and off cleanly in time.
HL-S02

Creative looping

Headliners use loops to reshape tracks: building their own intros and build-ups on the fly.

  • Extend a short intro: loop it to give more time for a long, controlled blend.
  • Create your own intro: find a sparse section, such as a riff or vocal in the breakdown, and loop it to use as an intro.
  • Build your own build-up: halve the loop length again and again (4, 2, 1, 1/2, 1/4 beats) to build tension, then hit a hot cue to drop the track.
  • Slip mode: with slip on, the track carries on underneath, so when the loop ends it's still in time.
Watch out

Without quantise, exiting a loop at the wrong moment pushes the track out of time with the other deck.

Students can
  • Create an intro from a section of a track.
  • Build tension with a shrinking loop and drop on the one.
HL-S03

Mixing acapellas

Mixing an acapella over an instrumental makes a live mash-up. The tempo, key, level and phrase all have to line up.

  1. Choose an instrumental, or an instrumental section, in a compatible key.
  2. Set the acapella to the same tempo as the instrumental.
  3. Cue it so its first full phrase lands on beat 1 of a phrase, allowing for any pickup.
  4. Start it on the right beat. If the pickup starts on beat 4, press play on beat 4 of the bar before.
  5. Balance the levels so it sounds like one record.
Tutor tip

Well-known vocals over unexpected instrumentals get the biggest reaction. If the original placement of a famous vocal is known, keep it.

Students can
  • Mix an acapella over an instrumental, in time, in key and in phrase.
HL-S04

Mixing between different tempos

Moving between genres at very different tempos is one of the hardest things a DJ does. There are four main ways.

1. Meet in the middle

Bring both tracks to a tempo halfway between them. From 140 to 160 BPM, mix at 150, then let the new track drift back to its own speed over the next phrase.

If either track would have to move more than about 6 to 8 percent, it starts to sound wrong. Use another method.

2. Cut

A clean cut on the phrase, often with an echo or reverb tail, works across any tempo gap.

3. Half time and double time

Some tempos fit together because one is double the other. Drum and bass at 174 BPM sits over hip hop at 87, and dubstep at 140 feels like 70. Beatmatch at the shared pulse.

4. Use a transition track

Let a track that changes tempo do the work for you (HL-K14).

Game

Tempo Ladder. Get from about 120 to about 170 BPM in as few clean transitions as possible, using at least two methods.

Students can
  • Mix between tracks with a large tempo gap using at least two methods.
  • Explain when meeting in the middle won't work.
HL-S05

Transform scratch

In a transform, the hand moves the sound slowly while the fader taps it in and out rapidly, chopping one long sound into a stream of short ones.

The fader starts closed. As the jog hand moves smoothly forward and back, tap the fader open briefly with the thumb or fingers, again and again. It's like patting your head and rubbing your stomach.

Students can
  • Perform a steady transform over a full stroke forward and back.
HL-S06

Flare scratch

The flare is the most advanced scratch in this handbook. The fader starts open and clicks closed briefly during each stroke, cutting one sound into two or more.

The jog hand moves forward and back steadily, like a baby scratch. The fader hand starts open and makes quick clicks shut and open again. A one-click flare splits each stroke into two sounds. Two clicks split it into three. The flare opens the door to fast, complex patterns.

Teach it
  1. Practise the click on its own: closed for an instant, then open.
  2. Add the jog hand slowly, one click per stroke.
  3. Move to two clicks per stroke when one is solid.
Students can
  • Perform a one-click flare in time.
  • Combine flares with other scratches in a short routine.
HL-S07

Hot cue performance

With hot cues on single sounds, the performance pads become a drum machine. Headliners use them to play new rhythms and chop vocals and melodies live.

Hot cue drumming

Set hot cues at the start of individual drum sounds, such as kicks, snares and hats. Then play the pads to create a new beat, over a beatless track or on its own.

  1. Start slowly with a simple pattern, using a metronome.
  2. Move to faster and swung or syncopated patterns.
  3. Load hot cues on two decks to layer sounds and trigger them together.

Chopping vocals and melodies

Set hot cues on individual words or notes and play them in a new order or rhythm.

Quantise and hot cues

Quantise makes hot cues land exactly on the beat, which helps accuracy. But it stops you playing between the beats, so turn it off for swung or syncopated patterns. Fix the beat grid first (MR-R02).

Colours and comments

In rekordbox, give hot cues colours by type (red for kicks, blue for vocals) and add comments, so the pads make sense during a performance.

Students can
  • Play a new drum pattern with hot cues.
  • Chop a vocal or melody into a new phrase.
Headliner

rekordbox

HL-R01

Streaming services

Streaming puts millions of tracks a tap away. It's powerful, but it isn't the same as owning your music.

rekordbox can connect to services such as Beatport, Beatsource, SoundCloud and TIDAL. Log in to the service from rekordbox's tree view with your account for that service, then browse and load tracks as normal.

AdvantagesDisadvantages
Huge library of musicNeeds a reliable internet connection
No need to store filesYou don't own the music
Try tracks before buyingMonthly subscription
Discover new music quicklyRecording streamed sets is usually blocked for copyright
Usually can't be exported to USB for club players
Tutor tip

Teach students to stream to explore, and buy the tracks they'll play. A set built only on streaming can fall apart if the wifi does.

Students can
  • Connect a streaming service and load a track.
  • Explain the pros and cons of streaming.
HL-R02

Stems

New

Stem separation splits a finished track into its parts, such as vocals, drums, bass and melody, while you play.

Newer versions of rekordbox and other DJ software can separate tracks into stems in real time. You can mute the drums to make an instant acapella, drop the vocal for an instrumental, or keep only the drums of one track under the melody of another.

Ways to use stems

  • Instant acapellas for mash-ups (HL-S03).
  • Cleaner blends: bring in only the drums of the next track, then the rest.
  • Remove a clashing vocal during a long blend.
Watch out

Stems need a recent computer and the right software version and plan. The separation isn't perfect, so check how it sounds on big speakers before using it in a showcase.

Students can
  • Use stems to create an acapella or instrumental live.
  • Blend using stems without obvious glitches.
HL-R03

Recording and reviewing a mix

Recording a mix lets students hear themselves as an audience would. Listening back is the fastest way to improve.

  • In rekordbox: use the recording function in performance mode. Recording may depend on the software plan.
  • On an all-in-one unit: many can record the master output straight to a USB stick.

Reviewing a mix

  1. Listen back without the decks in front of you.
  2. Note every moment that sounded off: a drift, a clash, a level jump.
  3. Pick the one thing that would most improve the mix.
  4. Practise just that in the next lesson.
Watch out

Only record a student's performance with prior permission, following NextGen's safeguarding guidance.

Students can
  • Record a mix and choose one specific improvement from listening back.
For every stage

Tutor toolkit

Assessment, games, safety and the words students need. Come back here whenever you need them.

Level-up assessment

A student levels up when you score every strand at 3 ("Secure") or above during the stage's check.

ScoreLabelWhat it looks like
1Not yetNeeds your help to do it
2Getting thereDoes it sometimes, with noticeable mistakes
3SecureDoes it reliably, with only small slips
4ConfidentDoes it easily, and makes their own choices with it

The six strands

StrandWhat you're looking for
TimingCounting, phrasing, beatmatching
Mix controlGain, levels, EQ, filters
TransitionsChoosing and executing the right transition
Performance techniquesCues, loops, scratching, juggling, effects
Selection and setsChoosing tracks, energy, reading the crowd
Knowledge and prepGenres, harmony, rekordbox preparation

Running the check

  1. Run it in a normal lesson when you judge the student ready. There's no fixed date and no failing: "not yet" just means more practice.
  2. Use the check described at the start of each stage, and score each strand.
  3. Tell the student their scores and one specific thing to work on, even if they've passed.
  4. Send the result to the office so it can be recorded and a certificate issued.

Certificates

Students who pass receive a NextGen certificate for that stage, presented at a showcase where possible. Certificates must not use the words "grade", "accredited" or "exam".

Watch out

Only record audio or video of a check with prior permission, following NextGen's safeguarding guidance. Your scores and notes are the standard evidence.

Games and challenges

Short games turn practice into play. Use one in the warm-up slot or as the end-of-lesson challenge.

GameSkillHow it worksStage
Find the OneTimingStart a track at random. The student claps on the next "one" within four bars.Warm-Up
Phrase SpotterTimingThe student calls "change" just before each new phrase. Count the hits.Warm-Up
Drift DetectiveTimingYou nudge one deck. The student says "ahead" or "behind", then fixes it.Warm-Up
Name That PartKnowledgeThe student taps along to the kick, then the clap, then the hats.Warm-Up
Energy Line-UpSelectionRank five tracks 1 to 5 for energy and justify one choice.Warm-Up
Hook SwapTransitionsBring each hip hop track in on its hook, on the phrase, with no vocal clash.Warm-Up
Call the BeatTimingYou call a bar and beat. The student claps exactly there.Main Room
Signal SpotterTimingName the signal at each phrase change: fill, riser, dropped beat or crash.Main Room
Screen OffTimingCover the displays and beatmatch two tracks of unknown tempo.Main Room
Crowd CardsSelectionFlip a crowd card. The student picks the next track and explains why.Main Room
Loop RescuePerformanceSave a mix by looping the outgoing track before it ends.Main Room
Scratch CopycatPerformanceCopy a one-bar scratch pattern, then swap roles.Main Room
Name That MachineKnowledgeName the source of an 808 kick, a 909 clap or a sampled break.Headliner
Tempo LadderTimingGet from about 120 to 170 BPM in as few clean transitions as possible.Headliner
Showcase Run-ThroughPerformingPlay the full set to the group. Feedback: two strengths and one thing to work on.Headliner
Tutor tip

Got a game that works? Send it to the office with its name, the skill it builds and how it works, and we'll add it to the next version.

Safety and good practice

These apply in every lesson, at every stage.

  • Hearing: keep headphone and speaker volume moderate, take breaks, and teach one-ear monitoring. Explain hearing loss and tinnitus, and why earplugs matter at gigs and festivals.
  • Levels: meters never in the red. Distortion damages speakers and sounds poor.
  • Kit: faders down before powering on, speakers on last and off first. Keep drinks well away from the decks, and coil cables safely.
  • Music sources: bought downloads or a DJ streaming service, never files ripped from video sites.
  • Age-appropriate music: use clean versions in school, and check lyrics before a track is played to a group or at a showcase.
  • Safeguarding: follow NextGen's safeguarding policy at all times. Don't contact students privately or connect with them on personal social media. Parent communication goes through the office, and lessons are only recorded with prior permission.

Kit and software

NextGen's standard setup is the DDJ-FLX2 controller with rekordbox, but every skill in this handbook works on any setup.

The skills transfer directly to other controllers, CDJs, turntables and software such as Serato or djay. Teach the skill first, then show where it sits on the student's setup.

Software features depend on the version and the student's subscription, so check before promising a feature. For home equipment questions, point families to the office for NextGen's current recommendations rather than suggesting specific products or prices.

Glossary

TermMeaning
AcapellaA vocal on its own, with no music
BarA group of beats, usually four in dance music
Beat gridThe markers software places on each beat of a track
BeatmatchingGetting two tracks to the same tempo, lined up beat for beat
BPMBeats per minute: the speed of a track
BreakdownA section where the drums drop out
Camelot wheelA numbered chart showing which keys sound good together
ClippingDistortion caused by a signal that's too loud
CrossfaderThe horizontal fader that blends between decks
Cue pointA saved starting point in a track
DropThe moment a track hits full energy
EQControls that turn the low, mid and high frequencies up or down
FilterRemoves frequencies above or below a set point
Gain or trimThe input level of a channel, set before the fader
Hot cueA saved point you can jump to instantly with a pad
KeyThe set of notes a track is built on
LoopA section of a track repeated continuously
PhraseA group of bars, often 8 or 16, after which the music changes
QuantiseSnaps cues and loops to the nearest beat
ReloadSpinning a track back and starting it again, also called a rewind
Slip modeKeeps the track running silently in time while you loop or scratch
StemsSeparate layers of a track: vocals, drums, bass, melody
TransientThe sharp attack at the start of a sound
TransitionMoving from one track to the next
